speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: THE BUDGET SPEECH TO BE DELIVERED MONDAY NEXT.
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my hon. friend is disappointed or not but circumstances have intervened which make it undesirable that the Budget Speech should be delivered to-morrow as was anticipated. One of the considerations in the matter is the pleasurable circumstance that the Prime Minister of the Dominion (Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden) is expected to take his place in the House to-morrow, and on account of his return just previous to the time that the Budget was to have been delivered it was not considered advisable to go on with the Budget without giving the Prime Minister an opportunity of looking over it. Secondly, we shall not sit on Thursday but shall sit on Friday. The Budget might have been delivered on Thursday if we had sat on that day, and it does not seem advisable to start the debate on Friday. The Budget will, however, be delivered on Monday next which must not be, for that week, considered as a dies non, as it very frequently is. It being Budget day I hope all the members will make it a point to be in their places.

maintopic: THE BUDGET SPEECH TO BE DELIVERED MONDAY NEXT.
speechtext: Monday is not usually Budget day. While I must not say that there has been no such case I have no recollection of a Budget ever having been delivered on Monday. It is usually considered desirable that the Budget should be delivered on a day when there is a pretty good attendance. Of course my right hon. friend will say that there should be a good attendance every day. Perhaps Monday is being chosen for some special reaspn that my right hon. friend has not given. He informs us that we are to have the pleasure of the presence of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and he immediately proceeds to say that is the reason why we should not have the Budget on Wednesday, implying that it will not be a pleasant thing and that he does not want to mix a pleasant and an unpleasant thing. I think my hon. friend might take into consideration the fact that Monday is not a Budget day, and it would be a wise thing to say Tuesday. If, however, the Government insists on Monday, we will have to agree to it.

maintopic: THE BUDGET SPEECH TO BE DELIVERED MONDAY NEXT.

The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) a day or so ago made inquiry as to wThether or not the Government had any official information respecting the migration of a large number of Mennonites from Manitoba and Alberta to the United (States, and if so, if the Government- was taking any steps to induce the people to remain in Canada?

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior) moved the third reading of Bill No. 57 to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was not aware frota the order of business given to the House last night that the third reading of this measure was to be moved this afternoon. However, I think it would be inadvisable to allow the Bill to pass its third reading without once again referring to features of the measure which seem to afford reasons why it should not pass in its present form. There has been a great deal of discussion on this Bill in committee and it is therefore unnecessary again to review in detail the different points that have already been mentioned. It will be sufficient to draw the attention of the House to significant features of these amendments.
The first amendment changes the method of making application for boards of conciliation and investigation. As I pointed out in committee the change in this regard

has not, so far as the Government has shown, been requested in any general way. The minister has intimated that members of the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress have asked for the change, but he has brought before the House no evidence in corroboration of his statement. He has not presented to the House any communications from the Trades and Labour Congress, and if he has them in his possession 1 would ask him to read them to the House before the Bill is passed. In the absence of any request for a change in the method of proceeding under the existing Act, I think it is obviously desirable that a method which has stood without criticism ior thirteen or more years should be permitted to stand, and that the effectiveness of the Act should not be jeopardized by an amendment of the kind suggested which can do no good and may lead to a great deal of harm.
Then another amendment changes the allowance to witnesses from what in the Act at the present time makes it accord with the allowance to witnesses in the courts of the different provinces and establishes instead a minimum of $4 a day. The effect of that amendment, as was pointed out in committee, will simply be to encourage large numbers of witnesses to be called before these boards, and will greatly increase the cost of administration. When this objection was pointed out to the minister, he made the somewhat popular reply that the Minister of Labour was anxious that workingmen should not be taken away from their work as witnesses and paid meagre witness fees. I might point out that many of these boards hold their proceedings after the day's work is over, and that the attendance of witnesses may be for only ten or fifteen minutes. If the law is not left as it is, it is certainly going vastly to increase the number of witnesses called and correspondingly increase the expenses of administration.
In considering the amount to be paid witnesses under the proposed amendment, we must also consider the effect of the previous amendment, which the Government has introduced, and which permits any two individuals connected with an industry to which the Act applies to go around with a memorial and upon securing signatures of a majority of the employees to become entitled to have a board of investigation granted. I believe that the two amendments taken together are going to have the effect of leading to a considerable
interference with many of these large industries which are among the most important to the country, and that they will prove prejudicial to capital and labour alike.
A further amendment gives to the Minister of Labour the power, before a strike or lockout has taken place, of his own initiative, and without request from any of the parties, to appoint a board of investigation under the Act. That, I believe, is going to work prejudicially to the Government, and to the parties whose interest it was intended to serve. The Act is intended as a means of investigating existing disputes, and provision is made whereby any of the parties interested may make application to the Government in a regular way for the appointment of a board. In the past that provision has worked very well. Interested parties have been able to get a board when it was needed. More than that, where a dispute in any case has assumed the proportions of a strike without a board having investigated its merits, the law, as amended two years ago, gives the right to the minister to step in at that stage and appoint a board on his own initiative. But here is an entirely new departure in the nature of interference by the Government of its own will with private business, and that I think is a principle which the House should not endorse.
These are the essential features of the outstanding amendments made by this Bill to the existing legislation. All of them are doubtful, some of them are thoroughly bad. Other amendments were asked for by labour and by the public for the protection of public interests, namely, that public services and industries in the nature of public utilities operated by municipalities or provincial governments should be brought under this law. The minister says that the Department of Justice has given some ruling in regard to the application of the Act to municipal enterprises, and in virtue of that ruling he does not propose to alter the measure one way or the other; he proposes to leave' these important matters in a condition of doubt. My view is that if instead of bringing in amendments altogether doubtful in their effect, the Minister of Labour had introduced amendments that are desired and have been requested for the protection of communities and of employees in these large public utilities, he would be rendering a service that would be worth while. There are these objections, it seems to me, to the amendments proposed to the Act, and, as already pointed

out, they cover pretty much all that the amendments pertain to.
Let me say that I think the discussion on these amendments has shown the necessity of having the Minister of Labour in this House. I wish to pass no reflection whatever on my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who has been piloting the Bill through the House. He has handled the measure with that skill which all are prepared to concede he possesses in very large measure. But I am sure he will be the first to admit that he has repeatedly felt the difficulty of appreciating the amendments which he was asking the House to accept. These industrial matters affect all classes, and if there is one place above another where a Minister of Labour should be it is in the House of Commons, where from day to day he can answer urgent questions on existing industrial situations.
It is a serious reflection upon the Government's appreciation of what is owing the public that as regards the two departments of government which have the most to do with questions of greatest concern to-day, namely, matters pertaining to labour and capital, and matters affecting returned soldiers, the ministers of those departments should be in the Senate where it is not possible for members of this House of Commons to ask them questions or to get the benefit of their views.
May I point out in this connection, Mr. Speaker, that the action of the Government in keeping the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment in the Senate amounts really to a form of closure so far as concerns the securing of information on vital questions or the discussion of them. We are by the rules of Parliament precluded from making any reference to what has taken place in the Senate. When those amendments to the Industrial Disputes Act were introduced in the Senate the Minister of Labour made certain representations concerning them. I have read the debate in the Senate. May I say that my hon. friend who has been piloting t'he Bill through this House gave us, in regard to this particular matter of witnesses' fees reasons for adopting the amendment, entirely different from those given by the Minister of Labour in the Senate. There the proposal originally was that the minimum should be $2 a day. In the discussion yesterday my hon. friend who sits to my right (Mr. Lemieux), an ex-Minister of Labour and the member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) also an ex-Minister of Labour, and the immediate pre-

decessor of the present minister and myself-three of us who have had to do with the administration of this Act, were all united as to the folly of making the suggested change, and yet there was no opportunity for the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) to give his views to the House, and under the rules we were precluded from referring to the debate in the Senate.

I want to ask the leader of the Opposition in view of what he has said, if, after all, he does not think it is desirable when a person or persons has or have a complaint to make that he or they should be in the position of an ordinary litigant, who upon issuing a writ is able to cite the defendant to appear before the court and have the whole case dealt with on its merits. In that way not only private interests but public interests are protected. Does the hon. gentleman not think that some such course as that should be taken?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to answer my hon. friend's question, but I am sorry to say that I do not quite see the point of it; I do not see that it has any bearing upon what I have just been, saying with regard to the importance of having the Minister of Labour in this House. I ishould be glad to have my hon. friend repeat his question if he cares to do so.

The hon. gentleman
has just said that he thinks it is unfair.
What? Louder.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon.
friend (Mr. Burnham) is referring to remarks which I made some little time ago, whereas I have in mind what I have just been saying.
Two minutes ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps a
little later I can go over the ground again, if my hon. friend wishes it. In the meantime, perhaps he will permit me to finish any remarks on this point of having the Minister of Labour in the House of Commons.
It is very opportune, Mr. Speaker, that reference should be made to this matter on this particular measure, because there is no doubt that the House has been detained longer in dealing with this measure than it would have been had the Minister of Labour been here to explain the features of his own Bill. We had to have two or three adjournments in order to find

out what the minister really meant. Lest it might be said by my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) that these adjournments were unnecessary, I should like to direct the attention of the House to the circumstance that I pointed out to the minister (Mr. Meighen) that one of the amendments which he brought in did away altogether with a very important amendment to this law which was passed in 1910. I asked him if he -were aware that that was the effect of his amendment, and he replied that he was not, and he adjourned the House to ask the Minister of Labour about it. Yesterday he came and frankly admitted that the amendment as brought in had that effect; that it was never intended as it dropped a very important amendment to the Act made in 1910 at the instance of the railway employees and railway companies. That, I think, is quite sufficient to show the unwisdom of having legislation promoted in this House by ministers who know nothing whatever in a detailed way about the legislation which they are promoting. But I come back to what is fundamental under the British system as respects a ministry and that is that it should be where at all times and on all occasions it can be questioned upon important matters of public concern. As I have said, the matters of greatest concern to the future prosperity and present contentment of our country, are those which relate to industry and to the well-being of returned soldiers.
The course of this legislation helps us to appreciate, I think, just why this session has lasted so long and why so little has been accomplished during the time we have been here. 'If any one looks over the legislation which the Government have introduced, he will find that almost the whole of it amounts to bringing into this *House Bills which have previously been brought in and passed, brought in again and amended, and then brought in once more for further amendment. I have not at the moment a list of the Bills which have been before the House; if I had I could show that with the exception of half a dozen measures, they are mostly in the nature simply either of a consolidation of former legislation or of a chopping up of existing laws into different Acts and the assignment of parts to one minister and parts to another, and the bringing in of little amendments, some of which may be necessary, but many of which, like the amendments' to which I have directed attention, are mischievous and bad. Now,
that is the reason why we have been taking up so much time during this session to so little account. There has been very little legislation of what one could call an original or constructive nature. The Government have brought forward practically nothing of that kind; if they think they have, I should like the minister to cite instances. Take the Grand Trunk Bill. At the last session that measure was introduced. We complained that it was being rushed through; that errors would creep in; that it would have to be amended on a subsequent occasion. This session the Government brings down a measure to correct errors in the' hasty legislation put through last session, and two or three days are occupied in the consideration of that measure. Take the Opium and Drug Bill. What was that measure but a measure that the Minister of Health (Hon. Mr. Rowell) had amended a year or two ago and which he brought back this session for further amendments-amendments so extensive that the whole Bill had to he reprinted? I might mention other legislation, but the facts are familiar to every hon. member. I submit that instead of tinkering and tampering with existing legislation to no effect, the time of this Parliament should be taken up, at this time of all times in the country's history, with constructive legislation along lines that are in accordance with the country's needs.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. N. W. Rowell (Minister of Health), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Canada Shipping Act, chapter one hundred and thirteen of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide:-

speakerposition: stagedirection

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext: Will the minister please explain how this changes the existing law as regards sick mariners?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext:
This does not change the existing law as regards provision for the care and treatment of sick mariners; it rather changes in some aspects the administration of the law, as I shall explain in a

moment, and it increases slightly the charges upon the vessels. Under the law as it stood up to the year 1908-09, the charge on vessels that came under the provisions of the Act was two cents per ton, in order to provide the money necessary for the care and treatment of sick mariners. In the year 1908-09, the charge was reduced to one and one-half cents per ton, and the amount thus realized was sufficient during the years between 1908 and the present year to provide ell moneys necessary for carrying on this branch of the Government service. But owing to the very substantial increase in the cost of hospital care, the revenue under the existing Act will not be sufficient to cover that cost. It is estimated, that the revenue this year will be approximately $75,000, and the expenditure this year will be something over $90,000. The change proposed by this resolution, viz.: to increase the charge fVom one and one-half cents to two cents per ton will it is estimated bring our revenue up to $90,000, or a little over which will be sufficient to provide the moneys necessary for the care and treatment of these sick mariners. The change in the amount of the fee is the most important change involved.
Then there is a change in administration. At the last session of Parliament, the administration of marine hospitals was transferred to the Department of Health. We had at one time ten marine hospitals; of these, four have been disposed of; two are not now in use; and at present only four are in operation. A change of policy has taken place in recent years in the administration of this branch of the service. In view of the limited number of patients to be treated at any given port, it has been found more economical to make arrangements with the local hospital authorities for their care and treatment on a certain per diem basis. The result has been that in a number of places the maintenance of these marine hospitals has been discontinued and satisfactory arrangements have been made with the local hospital authorities for the treatment of the patients. The bulk of the work, therefore, is now covered by arrangement with the local hospital authorities, and in dealing with the matter, it was the view of the two departments that it was more convenient, expeditious and satisfactory to administer the Government hospitals in association with the work which is carried on in hospitals with which the Government have agreements for treatment of patients. Therefore, it was decided that the whole work should be carried on under the Department of Health, and the necessary changes to make that administration effective are provided for in the proposed legislation. The result is a revision of the clauses of Part V of the Act, which simplifies the procedure for carrying on the work and puts under the Health Department, not only the management of the marine hospitals, but the care of the sailors who come into our ports and who are provided for in hospitals in Canada under agreement with the department at so much per diem.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext:
I think the minister should give careful consideration to this phase of the proposed change, namely, that we are increasing rather than decreasing, as it appears to me, the cost of administration. By subclause (a) the minister is given authority, with the approval of the Governor in Council, to rent and equip and maintain premises for hospitals for the care and treatment of sick mariners. While I do not object for a moment to any provision 'for giving proper care to sick mariners, I submit to the minister and the House that this is rather a wide provision. I think it would be exceedingly unwise to provide a method whereby at any chosen point hospitals could be opened up and maintained by the Government, when we know that in nearly every port affected by this legislation there already exists one or more properly equipped hospitals. I think the most effective and most economical way would be for the Government to make an arrangement .with the hospital authorities to take care of sick mariners at these hospitals. We should avoid as far as we can, increasing the cost of administration of this particular branch of the public service.
There is another point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Subclause (b) provides that there shall be levied and collected on every ship arriving in any port in Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, or British Columbia, a duty of 2 cents per ton. Why exempt Ontario? I am not offering this in any way as a criticism of Ontario, but the point I am making is that there must surely be occasions when there are sick mariners in Ontario, and if the country is to assume the responsibility of looking after sick mariners, I think the cost should be distributed as widely as possible. Why should vessels arriving at a port in Quebec, Nova Scotia or British Columbia be taxed, and ships arriving at ports on the Great Lakes in Ontario not taxed at all? 1 submit in support of that argument that there is in existence to-day

a very large unexpended sum from the fees which have been collected over many years. In other words, the cost of maintaining and caring for the sick mariners approximates less than one-half of the fees collected. I am not sure whether the fee is being increased by this measure.
I think this should be the course the Government should pursue. First of all, the 'fees should be reduced against shipping. I think that is of importance because after years of experience in caring for sick mariners we now have in hand a very large sum unexpended.
Another point I would bring to the attention of the minister is this. It is alleged -I am not sure whether the statement is accurate, and I would ask the minister to inform the House- that a large portion of the funds collected against shipping for the maintainence and care of sick marirers has been spent in other ways and for other purposes, purposes of relief and so forth, having no relation whatever to sick mariners. That is not fair. We must remember that this is a direct tax against shipping, and in so far as it is a tax against shipping, it is handicapping the shipping of this country.
Another important point is this: The sick mariners' dues imposed in Canada have in the past been seized upon by the American Government as a ground for imposing a retaliatory tax against Canadian shipping entering their ports. In British Columbia, for instance, and I presume the same thing applies to the Maritime Provinces as against the ports of Maine and other states, our ships going to Seattle are now taxed very much more heavily than we tax American ships. The Americans imposed that tax because we imposed a tax on American ships entering our ports under this provision for sick mariner's dues. In my opinion it would be better if, instead of imposing a tax against all shipping, thereby inviting these retaliatory taxes against our shipping, we provided that where seamen are taken from a ship ill, the shipowner or company should maintain and caTe for that seaman. I do. not think the shipping concerns of Canada are opposed to caring for sick mariners under Government control and direction, but to have a large fund created that is not used in anything like its entirety, and then under this legislation to increase the tax, is in my estimation bad policy for Canada, because this is a time above all others when we should encourage the development of Canadian shipping.

There is another point. Subclause (a) provides for the establishment of hospitals devoted exclusively to the treatment of sick mariners under the exclusive control and management of the minister. Supplementing what I said at the outset, I am afraid the minister will find, as the new Department of Health becomes established, that it is going to get far beyond anything that was anticipated 'by this House when it created that department. The care of sick mariners has been most admirably looked after by the Marine Department. The sick mariners have been well cared for in the past, as is proven by the fact that a large sum, amounting, I think, to several hundred thousand dollars for the 4 p.m. care of sick mariners remains unexpended. Now we cannot create new paraphernalia and new officials, and as this legislation suggests, possibly the establishment of Government hospitals in different parts of the country, without enormously increasing the expense. I assume that the minister has considered this but I must confess, Mr. Chairman, that in the brief time I have had to peruse the resolution it appears to me that we are establishing a very dangerous precedent which if extended and perpetuated will result in a tremendously increased cost to the country with no vital advantage to the sick mariner. After all it is merely the care of the sick mariner that we are interested in and not the establishment of an expensive institution in the country. I want the minister to understand that I am not approaching this question with the idea of embarrassing him at all but there is a very widespread feeling amongst the shipfping people that the cost to shipping should not be increased. One thing above all others that we should avoid is increasing taxes in any way unless we are going to get a very decided and advantageous return from the same. I bring these matters to the attention of the minister and I request not only an answer but if possible a careful reconsideration of his own views as expressed in the resolution.
.Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR:	This is largely a
question of administration. The Marine Department have been collecting large sums of money from the ships of this country but they have not been using that money for the treatment of sick sailors. They have been placing the money in the consolidated revenue fund and using it for other purposes. I went through the blue book a few days ago and discovered that they have between $150,000 and $200,000 still to the good.

They have collected over $150,000 from the shipping interests of this country for the purpose of treating sick sailors but they have not spent the money and they have not treated the sick sailors in very many cases. They have not undertaken the responsibility of looking after the sailors. There are	places	along	the	coast	ofNova Scotia where the department have not made	the necessary	provision	forattending to sick sailors. I drew the attention of the minister to one very urgent case in my own constituency. I do not know whether it is wise to transfer the treatment of sailors from the Marine Department to the Health Department. It would seem	at first	blush	that	it was	theproper thing	to do.	If we	are	to have	an
efficient Health Department it should look after the health of the people in all respects, but at the same time I fear that the Health Department, being situated at Ottawa and knowing so little about our sailors a thousand miles away, the sailors .may not receive any better treatment than they have been receiving in the past. I agree with the policy of the Government, whenever it is possible to carry it out, thal sailors should be treated at existing hospitals. Wherever there is an efficient hospital in the place where the sick sailor happens to be, it is the proper policy to make arrangement with the hospital to treat that sick sailor but I think that the department must also take the responsibility at places where there are no hospitals and that is the main difficulty along the Eastern coast of Canada. There are places so far distant from hospitals that it is very difficult to deal with cases of this kind. Take, for example, the town of Canso, which is situated some ninety miles away from the hospital at Douisburg which is the nearest hospital that is sufficiently equipped to treat a sick man. The hospital at Louisburg is one of the .four hospitals that the Department has been maintaining. We have about five thousand miles of coast line on the Eastern coast of Canada and you can understand that with only four marine hospitals these must be distant from any points where sailors may become ill. The policy of sending sailors to existing hospitals where there is sufficient equipment is the proper one.
I would like to see something done which will enable the minister to use the money that has been collected from these ships to equip hospitals or to assist in equipping hospitals at points like Canso where no hospital exists. Canso is the headquarters of the fishing fleet of Eastern Canada. It is
the nearest point to the Banks and hundreds of vessels come in there every year and there are many cases of hardship arising from the fact that there is no place there in which to treat sick sailors. The French Government have provided a hospital ship to look after the fishermen who have their headquarters at St. Pierre and it frequently happens, I understand, that the Canadian sailors are treated in the hospital ship belonging to France and treated free. Not having taken the same interest in our sailors, we have not made any provision of that kind at sea, and we have also failed to make provision on shore for those who come in. The minister should go a little further than he proposes. He has collected a very large sum of money from the shipping industry for the purpose of defraying expenses connected with this service. I think that he should make provision that in places like Canso-and there must be other places of the same kind- where no hospital exists some capital expenditure should be provided to assist in building and equipping a hospital. I understand! from the citizens of Canso that they are willing to do their best to maintain an efficient hospital at that place and in addition to treating their own sick they iwill be pleased to treat the sailors who ought to be treated by the department. They are not able to do that under present conditions. They have no hospital and in order to procure the money to build and equip a hospital it will be necessary to give them some assistance. I would like to ask the minister if he would agree to some policy whereby capital assistance could be given, or a yearly amount could be provided for a sufficient number of years, to enable a small town like Canso to build and maintain an efficient hospital.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext:
I observe in the resolution that there is an exception made in the case of the province of Ontario. Am I right in believing that the province of Ontario is exempt from this resolution? I understand that the Government has been collecting fees for sick sailors for many years. In the province of Ontario we have as many sick sailors proportionately as there .are on the sea coast. If there is a sick sailor in Ontario he is taken off the ship and sent to a local hospital where he is attended to. The expense is not charged against the ship; it is charged against the municipality. In the largest town in my riding, Colling-wood, they have a marine and general hospital where they treat sailors who come from various places to that port. They are

sent to the port and treated in the hospital, and the municipality invariably has to pay all the charges as these sailors have very little money. In many instances they are suffering from contagious diseases, such as smallpox, and they are sent to the hospital and quarantined and some are treated for five or six months. In typhoid fever cases they are taken care of for two or three months. Whilst the Dominion Government assesses shipping and receives a large mount annually from that source for the purpose of attending sick sailors, not one dollar have I ever been able to get out of the Marine Department for a hospital. The minister might take notice of that. Not only is that the case in Collingwood but it is equally true in respect to Midland, Fort William, Port Arthur, Goderich, Kincardine, St. Catharines, Toronto and all those points on the Great Lakes. There are over four thousand sailors under ordinary circumstances on Canadian ships on the Great Lakes . who need this attention. Not only do we have to attend to the Canadian sailors hut a great deal of the traffic goes by American ships and we have to attend to the crews of those vessels as well. The American vessels come to our great lake ports with corn, iron ore, and other products. Many of them are allowed to engage in the coasting trade in Canada and they come to Fort William, Midland St. Catharines, Port Colborne, and other places with grain. Their sick men have to be attended to and why should Canadian municipalities have to meet the expense? That is something I -.annot understand and I would like to know from the minister when he makes his reply whether it is a .fait that this money tax has been collected from the shipowners on the Great Lakes in recent years and if so why it has non been paid over to these hospitals for the work they have done. -I think that in the case cf the hospital in Collingwood it will be found that there has been some seven or eight thousand dollars of charges against sailors who entered that hospital in the last four or five years. The money was handed over by the ships for the maintenance of these hospitals but the municipality has been unable to collect a cent of it and the reason assigned is that the municipalities are attending to the matter. For the reasons I have given I cannot understand what induced the minister to insert a clause in the Act exempting Ontario from the operation of this law. The Department of Marine for years has known that we have been making a claim for this 
money. The hon. member (Mr. Duff) shakes his head.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext: The shipowners in Ontario have not paid these dues before.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext: I would like to know why they have not been made to pay the dues the same as the ships in the other provinces?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext:
They claim the charges are too high.
Mr. CURRIE.: The charges are not too high for other purposes. A charge is made by the Federal Department, for example, for inspection. Shipowners have to pay a fee for inspection to the province as well and they even have to pay an inspection fee to some foreign association; they pay to that association $35 or $40 for certificates of that character. There is no reason in the world why the shipowners on the Great Lakes-and they are not all Canadians, some are Americans, because there are foreign vessels trading on the Great Lakes * -should not be charged the necessary fees to maintain hospitals for sick sailors. Those sailors are very subject, for instance, to typhoid fever. They are more subject to that disease than are the sailors on the ocean; and most of these cases in the Lake hospitals will be found to be typhoid fever cases. Up to a few years ago-I do not know whether there is any stringent rule against it now-these ships used to pump the water for drinking purposes on board from the slips at Toronto and various other ports which they entered, and by reason of the fact that sewage was discharged there instead of being carried a long distance out, that drinking water very often was contaminated. The same difficulty does not exist on ocean vessels because they either get pure water from the land before they start on their voyages, or else use salt water which has been condensed. As a result of these outbreaks of typhoid, the Department of Marine was compelled to order the installation of systems whereby the drinking water was disinfected before it was supplied to the sailors. The outbreaks of disease became so bad at _one time that about 15 or 20 per cent of sailors on board the ships were suffering from typhoid fever because of the conditions which I have mentioned. I have every sympathy with the shipowner, but I have more sympathy with the poor sailor who never gets much of a deal from anybody, even from the Government. He is asked to pass examinations but the Government does

not provide any education for him. Take the man who has to undergo an examination for the position of marine engineer. He is required to take a very high standing in mathematics and thermodynamics but no government in this country is giving men an education along such lines or conducting schools where these men might receive a training for their calling. It is like pulling hen's teeth to get a dollar out of the Government for assistance towards any of these purposes. Now this legislation gives the last blow-this is the blow that killed father. None of this money is to go to the province of Ontario but it is to be left to the farmers in the rural districts and the artisans in the towns to bear the expense of ministering to our Lake sailors whenever they fall sick. I hope the minister will see that the clause is amended so that the cities of Toronto, Hamilton, St. Catharines, Kingston, and others along the Great Lakes that have been maintaining hospitals for sick sailors and saying very little about it are properly compensated for the services they render. It should not be a case of charity at all to have to attend the sick sailors. The shipowners are very wealthy. Some of these shipping companies are paying as high as 80 per cent per annum since the beginning of the war. Talk about profiteering! Therefore to continue to exempt them from the payment of $35 or $40 per ship per year is to my mind a great mistake. I hope the minister will take that into consideration and will amend the clause so as to bring all the provinces under the same regulation and see that the sailors on the Great Lakes get just as good and fair a chance as the sailors on the ocean.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext: I have listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) and I cordially agree with a great many of them. But the trouble of which he complains is due to the fact that the sailors on the Great Lakes are not looked after by the Department of Marine or the Department of Health, because there is no provision for that purpose.

speechtext: American sailors who are taken sick are looked after by the United States.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-'SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext:
I am not discussing what the United States Government are doing, I am
referring to what we do in Canada. As I said a moment ago I am in perfect agreement with many of the hon. gentleman's remarks and am only trying to get this matter straightened out. If the hon. gentlemen will look at clause 384 of the Shipping Act he will see that it reads:
There shall be levied and collected on every ship arriving in any port in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island or British Columbia, a duty of two cents for every ton which such ship measures, registered tonnage.
It will be seen that the province of Ontario is omitted from the operation of the Act. As far as I am concerned I will be quite satisfied to have the Act made applicable to that province. I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman says: There is no reason why sick sailors in the province of Ontario should not be treated in exactly the same manner as are the sailors on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and on the gulf of St. Lawrence. I feel quite confident that ship owners on the great lakes will not object to paying the small amount of dues which the Government asks in connection with the Sick Mariners Fund. Two cents per ton on a ship of 10,000 tons means $200. That has to be paid three times a year so that in the case of a vessel of that tonnage the ship owner would only have to pay $600 to ensure that sick sailors shall be properly looked after in the hospital. If the province of Ontario comes under this Act the department will arrange either that the local hospitals shall care for the sick sailors on the Great Lakes, or else will maintain hospitals of their own where the men can be treated.
Looking over this resolution and comparing it with the old Act, part V, chapter 113 of the Shipping Act, I really cannot see that there is very much difference between them except that the wording of the resolution is much longer than the part V referred to. If the Government finds it necessary to put the care of sick mariners under the Department of Health instead of under the Department of Marine, the wording of the Act will require to be changed and "Minister of Health" substituted for "Minister of Marine" in clause 5. Personally I am opposed to the care of sick sailors going under the Health Department; I am firmly convinced that it is purely a marine matter and should be left in the hands of the Marine Department. In the last fifty years the department has built up a good branch in connection with this work, and the officials appointed to look after the marine

hospitals are well qualified and capable men, and give satisfaction not only to the general public and the shipowners but to the sailors themselves. It seems to me therefore that to transfer the care of the marine hospitals to the Department of Health would be a mistake. The Department of Health will, in a few years, have sufficient work to do without bothering in any way with the sailors who come under this Act.
I also notice that in subsection (e) it is provided:
That as regards fishing vessels, the duty shall not be payable on ships employed exclusively in fishing or arriving at a port in the provinces when on a fishing voyage, but the master or person in command of a ship registered in Canada used exclusively in fishing or to be employed on a fishing voyage, may, if he so desires, pay the said duty of two cents for each registered ton before the said ship makes its first fishing voyage in any year, at the first port at which the ship receives any part of her outfit for the said voyage, and thereafter before each subsequent voyage during the year, but not exceeding three payments in all in any calendar year.
In my opinion this clause ought to be changed so that there would be no discrimination against fishing vessels as compared with coasting or foreign-going vessels. Of course under the clause the fees may be paid if the captain or owner so desires; but it seems to me better to have the fishing vessel treated in the same manner as the coasting or foreign-going vessel, and there is no reason why this should not be done. As I said a moment ago the owners of fishing vessels have paid these fees willingly because they realized the benefits which the Marine Department have -been able to give sick mariners. I suggest that the clause be changed so that fishing vessels be treated in exactly the same manner as other vessels.
I was very much interested in what the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) said as to what is going on on the Nova Scotia coast. I do not wish to say anything about the county of Guysborough, but I do say there is pressing necessity for a marine hospital at the Port of Canso-not so much perhaps for the fishermen of Guysborough county as for the fishermen and sailors on the Atlantic coast. As the hon. member for Guysborough well said, Canso is the half-way house for fishing and coasting vessels going from the different parts of Nova Scotia to Newfoundland or the gulf of St. Lawrence. There is hardly a day in the shipping season when there are not from ten to twenty-five vessels either anchored in the Port of <Canso or passing up the strait of 
Canso, and those vesels sometimes have to land sick men at this port. It has been a great inconvenience to those sick men to have to be sent all the way to the Hospital at Halifax or to their homes. Some one has said that the Government has on hand $150,000 collected from ship-owners _ of this country which has been paid into this fund. It seems to me that Parliament should immediately take steps to erect a marine hospital at Canso -for the treatment of sick mariners. Therefore I would strongly urge on my -hon. friend who is in charge of this Bill (Mr. Rowell) that immediate steps he taken to that end. If there is one port in Canada where something should be done for sick mariners it is at the port of Canso.
The department should also arrange to have a hospital ship. If I may be allowed to refer to what I said some time ago on a resolution before the House. I then suggested that one of the things the Government should do to encourage our fishing industry was to have hospital ships stationed at different -ports on the Nova Scotia coast or on the Banks to look after sick mariners. It seems to me that the Government might very well arrange to have a hospital ship placed at the disposal of sick mariners on the Atlantic coast, and also, if necessary, on the Pacific coast, where there is also a great fishing industry.
Suggestions have been made to close the present hospitals and arrange with local hospitals to look after sick mariners. While there may be some advantages in such an arrangement, I am not very strongly in favour of it. In my opinion it will very greatly increase the expenditure of the department, and I feel that sick mariners require rather different treatment, perhaps, than other sick people. Usually they are landed from their ship, and they will very likely be-
Mr. CURRIE; What would the hon. member do in case of contagious disease? Supposing two or three men are taken off a ship suffering from plague or small-pox, should not the department have power to equip a place in which to take care of those men? Some one has to do that.
