Mr. ,DUFF: There is something in what my hon. friend says, but when members on this side make suggestions, the Government usually answer that they have to give them their most serious consideration. If I leave what I intend to say on this provision until we are in committee on the Bill, I may be given that answer, so that if the committee will bear with me for a moment, I shall bring the minister's attention to this matter so that he may consult his officials and propose a change in conformity with my views and the views of a number of ship owners in different parts of the country.
Under the present Act a vessel which is chartered to go to North ,Sydney or Sydney and load coal for St. Johns, Newfoundland, and then to proceed to Europe, the West Indies or South America, may not
[The Speaker.]
participate in the sick mariner's fund or the benefits of the marine hospital if a sailor on that ship gets sick, say, at North Sydney-that is to say, while the vessel is on a voyage from one port in Nova Scotia to another port in Nova Scotia. I respectfully suggest that a change be made in clause .(d) with a view to providing that when a vessel is not on what is known as a local voyage but is chartered to go to a foreign port and calls at a local port for cargo, that vessel may participate in the benefits provided by the Act.
There is another clause which, I think, should not be in the Bill to be founded on the resolution, that is, section 2 of the resolution. Clause 2 repeals section 207 of the present 'Shipping Act, which section deals entirely with payment of expenses in connection with shipwrecked or distressed mariners who may find themselves in foreign ports and has nothing to do with sick mariners. The minister no doubt knows that, under the present Shipping Act, owners of vessels have to pay the expenses of shipwrecked or distressed steamers. For instance, supposing a vessel is wrecked off' the Atlantic coast and the crew are taken to Portugal or Spain, immediately on their arrival at any port, the crew go to the British Consul who arranges to send them home. An account of all expenses incurred in sending them home is sent to the Marine Department at Ottawa, which collects the amount from the owners of the vessel that was wrecked, Therefore, this clause has nothing to do with sick mariners, and should not come under the Department of Health, but should be left as it was before under the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I suggest to the minister that he take that clause into consideration, drop it from the resolution, and arrange that the matter be left in the hands of the Marine Department, where it has been for many years.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT-SICK AND DISTRESSED MARINERS.
speechtext: I do not wish to delay the passage of the resolution, but I think it my duty, at the present stage of the proceedings, to call the attention of the minister to the very strong protest which he has received from the Shipping Federation. This protest is headed "Sick Mariners' Dues." Reference was made to this protest this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and as I am one of the representatives of the city of Montreal, I think it is only due to the Shipping Federation that I should bring their protest to the attention of the House and to the country. This imposition

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
of a tax upon vessels for the
5 p.m. Sick Mariner's Fund has caused a retaliatory measure to be passed by-the United States, and it is very striking that whilst in Canada American vessels are taxed for that fund to the extent of only four and one-half cents per annum, our vessels, as a result of this tax, when they reach any of the United States ports, are taxed to the extent of 37 cents *per ton per annum. Therefore, it is, I believe, in the interest of all, if we wish to help our merchant marine and to develop our Canadian trade abroad, that consideration be given to the protest of the Shipping Federation against that taxation. The minister received on May 7 a memorandum from the manager and secretary of the Shipping Federation, Mr. Thomas Robb, and with your permission, Mr. Chairman, 1 shall read just the principal paragraphs which deal with this question. Mr. Robb says:
I am directed on behalf of the members of the Shipping Federation of Canada (Incorporated) who represent 900,882 tons of shipping trading to the St. Lawrence to respectfully protest against the proposed amendment you intend making to the Canada Shipping Act under Part V thereof covering sick and distressed mariners, particularly in reference to increasing the duty from 1} cents to 2 cents per ton per voyage.
The Federation for years past have been striving to have this unjust tax removed which has proved a discrimination not only against the St. Lawrence route, tout also against the Trade and commerce of the Dominion, and as a result of these protests, the Government reduced the duty from 2 cents to 1} cents per ton. From your notice of motion, the Federation presume it is the Government's intention to increase this tax to 2 cents per ton, and I have the honour of submitting herewith the views of the Federation why this tax should not he further increased, but also why it should be abolished in its entirety:
1.	The tax now imposed is 1J cents per ton registered restricted to three voyages in one year. The accumulated surplus of the fund from figures taken from Government returns amounts to $294,996.08, while the surplus for the year 1917 amounted to $12,011.81.
2.	The tax is an unjust impost in itself and is ur known in other countries with the exception of Turkey and Peru, which in itself shows a sufficient reason for the Canadian Government abolishing the tax.
3.	The levying of this tax on the Province of Quebec, Maritime Provinces and British Columbia, is the cause of a retaliatory tonnage tax being imposed against tonnage hauling from these provinces by the United States. Moreover, sick mariners' dues are not levied in the Province of Ontario. Tonnage from that province goes free both in home ports and in the United States which is an unfair discrimination against the other provinces.
4.	Shipowners are liable for hospital or funeral expenses for seamen injured or killed in service, and for medical attendance, medi-
144}
cine and wages while incapacitated from duty by sickness during the voyage, and the Canadian Government is fully protected by sections 207 and 208 of the Merchants Shipping Act, which are to be found in the Statutes of Canada, 58 and 59 Victoria, volumes 1 and 2, pages 116 and 117, and being already provided for it is unfair and unjust that vessels trading to Canadian ports should be further taxed to supply funds for other purposes, and further, there is no just reason why one vessel should he taxed to support the sick of another.
The Federation understand that one of the difficulties the Government have had in dealing with this matter is in regard to sick seamen on transient vessels. This we respectfully point out to you can be easily overcome by you instructing the. collectors of Customs that when any seamen may require to be cared for in Canadian hospitals, the master of any transient vessel shall he required to give a bond for an amount to cover any expenses that may be incurred in connection with the sick seamen who may be left in hospital. This can be required of the captain or the owners' responsible representatives before clearance is granted to the vessel by the customs authorities, and if this was carried out it would entail little or no extra duty to the collectors of Customs.
5.	The moneys collected from this tax have not been applied for the purposes for which it was collected. A return made to Parliament in 1888 shows that since Confederation, the sum of $236,500 had1 been applied to other purposes, chiefly for the relief of the sick poor in the cities of Quebec, Kingston and St. Catharines.
6.	The Federation do not wish to avoid or saddle the Government in any way with the cost of providing for the sick mariner, but say that each vessel should be required to pay and look after her own sick in the same manner as is done in other countries, thus relieving the Dominion Government of any legal or moral responsibility to care for the sick seamen any more than for other Sick people.
The seventh paragraph deals with British Columbia, and as my hon. Ifriend (Mr. Stevens) has explained the situation as regards that province, I shall not quote this paragraph.
The members of the Shipping Federation of Canada, being the largest payers of these dues, trust that this just grievance of theirs will receive full and fair consideration, and that the minister will introduce an Act during the present session of Parliament abolishing this unfair tax, which will be another step in the direction of freeing the Canadian tonnage from the retaliatory tonnage dues in the United States.
Such is the protest of the Shipping Federation, one of the largest corporations in Canada, and one whose interests are welded to the general trade of this Dominion.
There are two or three essential facts which, in my humble judgment, should not be lost sight of by my hon. friend when we consider the Bill. It should strike the members of the committee, on general principles, that the law as it stands to-day concerning the sick mariners' fund, is an-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
tiquated, and requires to be radically changed. It is not fair, for instance, that these dues should be collected from the ships in one province and not from the ,ships in another province. I always understood my bon. friend the Minister of Health and hon. gentlemen opposite to be in favour of uniformity in the laws ,of this Dominion. Now, if there is one law which should foe uniform throughout this country, i't is this law concerning the dues collected for the sick mariners' fund. There should not be one mode of taxation in one province, and another in another.
A second consideration which strikes me as very important indeed, is the fact that we are all willing that in the years to come great efforts should be made to develop our trade abroad and to seek wider markets for our products. Now it seem*-to me, as Mr. Robb states in this correspondence, that if we are charging per cent per ton on foreign ships, while we are met by a retaliatory tax of 30 cents per ton per annum by our greatest trade rival, the United States, we are defeating the end we have in view, because this will tend to restrict rather than to expand our trade. It is a restriction of trade, and I call my hon. friend's attention to the seriousness of the matter. I have no special brief for the Shipping Federation, but as my hon. friend the Minister of Marine knows, its members are all working hard to develop the trade of this Dominion. I know nearly all the members of the federation, and I know they do not wish to be debarred from the privilege of paying taxes. Far from it; they pay their full share of the taxes of this country. They arc willing to help the Government in developing and expanding the trade of this Dominion, but they call the attention of the Government to the injustice of this particular tax, and it seems to me it is only wise on the part of the Government to do away with this antiquated legislation, and to establish a uniform system throughout all the provinces. It is not fair that ships in the Maritime Provinces, in the neighbouring province oif Quebec, and in British Columbia should be taxed, while ships in Ontario are exempt. It gives the ships from Ontario an unfair advantage over the ships from other provinces when they reach American ports. I hope, therefore, when we consider the Bill the minister will take into serious consideration the protests which he has received. I am very anxious to know what are his views on this question.
[Mr. Lemieux.l

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I have already intimated, when the Bill is in committee there will be the fullest possible opportunity of discussing its provisions in detail. I shall not this afternoon therefore take up the time of the committee with going into the matter in detail, but shall only briefly refer to some of the observations and suggestions made by the hon. members of the House.
Dealing with them in order, with reference to the point made by my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) as to the position of Ontario under the Bill, the explanation is that this has been the law ever since Confederation. I think the reason why Ontario is exempt is the distinction drawn in our Shipping Act, and in the American Shipping Act, between ships sailing on purely inland water and ocean-going vessels. As the ships sailing purely on inland lakes are carrying on a traffic on the inland lakes alone, they are not brought within the provisions of this part of the Shipping Act. They are neither taxed, nor are the sick mariners on these ships on the inland lakes of Ontario entitled to be provided for out of the fund. Neither the shippers nor the mariners come within the scope of the Act, and they have not done so since Confederation. The Act in that respect is just the same as it has been ever since we have had a Shipping Act.

My hon. friend will
understand that I do not begrudge Ontario her good fortune in not being taxed. I am simply asking that the province of Quebec and the Maritime Provinces and British Columbia be put on a footing of equality with Ontario so far as this exemption is concerned. 1 want the system to be uniform throughout all the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All I have been doing
is endeavouring to make clear to the House the reason why the provision is as it is. One further remark in reference to it. My hon. friend's suggestion that vessels going from Ontario to maritime ports or American ports on the sea coast will be exempt from these dues, is due to a misapprehension. That is not the case. It is only vessels plying on these inland waters, and not those that pass out of these inland wraters to the ports of Quebec or to ocean ports that are exempt. I am quite prepared to say that when the Bill comes into committee this matter may receive further consideration.
It may be that the change could not be made without some consequential amend-

ments to the general Shipping Act. It is a matter that would have to be very carefully considered in all its bearings before an important departure of that kind could be made. I recognize that mariners sailing upon the inland lakes are entitled to the fullest protection and I am anxious to eee that they get it. Then, in reference to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and also contained in the memorandum from the Shipping Federation that there is a large accumulated surplus to the credit of the "Sick Mariners' Fund," I beg now to say that there is no such surplus standing to the credit of this fund. The monies collected have been paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, they have been expended from year to year and the way the figures which my hon. friend has read, or any figures showing a surplus, is arrived at is by taking the actual disbursements in connection wkh the marine hospitals and the payments to other hospitals on the one hand and subtracting those from the receipts on the other. But I would like to point out to my hon. friend that that method of computation does not take into consideration at all the cost of administering this fund by the staff which has existed in the Marine Department and which has now bee ntransferred to the Department of Health. If the actual cost of administration was charged up against the fund, my information is that there would be no surplus whatever to its credit. The fact is that at the present time there is no fund and that in order to dift-eharge the obligations which accrue cn account of these sick mariners at the different hospitals where they are being treated it is necessary that we should have more money than we are now receiving. That is the reason for asking for the increased grant.	.

Is it not true that for
many years past the revenues of this fund have far exceeded the expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I intimated to my
hon. friend, if you leave out all cost of administration-yes. The figure which has been used has not taken into consideration the cost of administration and I am not sure that it takes into consideration the money spent on capital account. My information is that if you charged against this so-called fund-there is no fund in fact existing-it is a name rather than a fact-the amounts that might properly be charged against it, there would be no surplus. There is no surplus to-day. This year
we will run behind some thousands of dollars by reason of the increased amounts we must pay the hospitals for the treatment of these patients and I am assured that the rates in the new schedule are simply equal to the cost of carrying on the work. My hon. friend suggested the possibility of increased expenses of administration. There is absolutely no change as far as that is concerned by way of additions to the staff. The staff which has been administering this branch of the service in the Department of Marine and Fisheries has been transferred to the Department of Health and this same staff is carrying on the work and there is no thought or intention of increasing it. As I have already intimated, the policy of the Government is not to construct new hospitals but rather to take advantage of existing hospitals and make a suitable arrangement for the treatment of patients. I am glad to say that the hospitals of the country have been reasonable and that we have been able to conne to a reasonable arrangement with them for the treatment of these sick mariners.
The provision in the Bill in reference to maintaining hospitals but carries forward in substance the provisions of the old law which permits us to carry on the hospitals which we own. The details of that can be explained when we go into Committee on the Bill. My hon. friend from North 6im-coe (Mr. Currie) referred to the situation in Ontario and the monies charged against the municipalities for the maintenance of these sick mariners. I shall be glad to inquire into that matter and ascertain what the position is. The situation in Ontario however differs in one respect from that with regard to seamen upon the high seas. I believe that these ships upon our inland lakes come under the Ontario Workmen's Compensation Act, that is a matter which I shall be glad to look into. I should think that they would come under the Workmen's Compensation Act.

No American ships come
in, they have men hurt and they do not come under the Workmen's Compensation Act.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. But our ships do, I understand, in British Columbia. However that is a matter that I will look into before the Bill goes into committee with a view to considering that aspect of it. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has suggested that fishing vessels be brought under the operation of the Act and required to make the payment and become entitled to the benefits the same as the

merchant vessels. As far as the department is concerned, if that is the view of the House, we have not the least objection to it. When, the matter goes into committee I shall be glad to know what the view of the House is in that respect.
In reference to the point raised by the hon. member 'for Vancouver and also referred to by the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) in connection with the memorandum from the Shipping Federation, that the result of our imposing this tax upon ships is that there is a retaliatory charge against our ships in American ports, may I say that the first I knew of that fact, if it be a fact, was when I read the memorandum from the Secretary of the Shipping Federation. It is my intention to look into that matter and see upon what foundation the statement rests. It does not appear to be reasonable to suppose that because we impose this very limited tonnage tax for the purpose of looking after sick mariners there should be a retaliatory charge of some thirty cents per ton. That is a matter that I shall carefully look into with a view to ascertaining what the situation is and it can be considered when the Bill goes into committee.

For the benefit of the minister I might point out that if a ship leaves Vancouver and goes to Seattle and a sailor falls sick in Seattle the ship has to pay the cost of the sailor's treatment in Seattle although it paid the sick mariner's dues in Vancouver. The ship can get no return from the department. I think there might be some provision to meet a case of that kind.
There should be a reciprocal arrangement in a matter of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid the matter which my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) has mentioned could not be dealt with by our legislation. 'If >some reciprocal arrangement could be established, the situation might be relieved in that way. We would be glad to give the matter consideration. In reference to the observations of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I would suggest that the question of how any particular amount should be expended is more properly a question for the Estimates rather than in connection with this proposed legislation. My hon. 'friend has brought the question to my attention and I am having a report made on the local situation. When we go into committee on the Estimates, the matter may be further discussed. I shall ask that the committee

report the resolution and further discussion can take place upon the Estimates.

I desire to draw the attention otf the minister to the fact that there is no provision in this Bill for any capital expenditure. There is a provision here for treating sick sailors and even for renting buildings for hospitals; but what is needed in the case of Canso is some provision for capital expenditure for an hospital. I would therefore suggest that the expenditure by the Government be made conditional-I see no reason why that should not be done. So that the town of Canso, or any other town similarly circumstanced that will give a certain amount per year might then be entitled to receive something from this fund. I know pretty well that if you assist hospitals indiscriminately from the fund you will have no end of trouble, and I do not want to put the department in that position. I would suggest that where there is a small town at some distant point on the coast that will contribute an amount say $500 per year, out of its own taxes for the purpose of maintaining and establishing a marine hospital for the treatment of their own sailors that we should give a similar sum. I would like to see the minister amend the resolution so as to make provision for capital expenditure in that way at a place where no hospital at present [DOT]'exists.
In regard to the situation at Washington, and the possibility of a retaliatory tax, has the minister heard anything from our Trade Commission on the question of retaliation? That is a matter that would properly come within the province of the commission, and if its members were alive to their duties I would think the minister would have some report from them on the subject, because a realiatory tax of thirty cents per ton on our shipping would be a very heavy tax.
I would again ask the minister to consider whether he will not amend his resolution in such a way as to enable something to be done towards establishing a hospital in places where there is no hospital at present. For many years the custom has been for the captain of a ship to put his sick sailors ashore at Canso but unfortunately there is no one to take the responsibility of providing a place in which those men may be cared for. Sometimes they are treated in a dwelling house where there is no suitable accommodation, and men have lost their lives because in that particular place there was no proper treatment available for them. I think the department ought to find a solution for that problem and that my

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: solution is a reasonable one. Let the Government make a proposal to the town of Canso, or any other town in the same situation, and say: " We will give you for ten years a capital expenditure of so much per year, if you will levy the same amount upon yourselves so as to build and maintain a hospital which will permit of the treatment of your own sick and also any sailors that may require to be treated there."
What is the population of the town of Canso P
About 2,000.

If the resolution passes in its present form there is no possible way in which, when the Bill founded upon it comes before the House, the minister can give consideration to the facts which I brought to the attention of the committee this afternoon with reference to the province of Ontario. Because it could be pointed out when the Bill came forward for consideration that there is a distinct clause in the resolution declaring that no money is to be spent on the provinces of Ontario and Quebec for this purpose. I would therefore suggest that clause '(d) be struck out, and also that the word "Ontario" be inserted in clause (b) so as to make the Act apply in that province as well as the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia. The old law on this subject passed many years ago with respect to this matter did not apply to the province of Ontario because there was no ships of any size that were owned or operated in that province. I believe that three or four wooden vessels of a comparatively small total tonnage would cover all the shipping in operation in that province in the time to which I refer; but to-day ships of tern and eleven thousand tons are built and big fleets of large vessels employing a great number of men are plying on the Great Lakes. If the resolution is not amended in committee now, it will not be legally possible to do anything in the way of granting relief for the province of Ontario. I would therefore suggest to the minister that the resolution be amended in the way I have suggested. Then if his information is such as to warrant him in bringing the province of Ontario under the provisions of the Act it will not be necessary to come back and introduce another resolution. I would make that suggestion to the minister and I hope the committee will sustain him if he agrees to make the change, because I am satisfied the intention of Parliament is
to help our sailors no matter in what province they may be employed.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend's objection is valid-that is that we could not .amend the Bill in the way suggested-the same objection would apply to the resolution. We cannot amend a resolution if that amendment adds to the burden of taxation, it would be necessary to have a supplementary resolution to which His Excellency has assented. I therefore suggest that the resolution should go through in its present form.
I am quite willing that this matter, which affects Ontario, should be further discusssed when the Bill is before the House, and if the conclusion is reached that it is proper to make the suggested change I will introduce Whatever supplemental resolution may be necessary to carry it into effect. However, we will have to consider that carefully.

The minister must know that a resolution of this kind when it goes into committee is subject to change and there is no harm in making such a change. Parliament is supreme on a matter of this kind and all that I am asking is that this particular clause (d) be dropped. If we were making any addition to it possibly there might be some force in the suggestion that the resolution involved greater expenditure than was contemplated, and that it had not received the authority of the Governor General. I do not, however, see why the suggestion could not be carried out under the rule. There is nothing wrong with my proposition, it is customary for the House to do as proposed, and it is one of the prerogatives of the House to be able to change money bills. With the consent of the Government the House can at any time advance or reduce any expenditure contemplated in a money bill.

I think that the point taken by the President of the Privy Council is well taken. There could be no objection to the insertion of the word "Ontario," but that would undoubtedly broaden the taxation power of this resolution which, as proposed does not contemplate levying any taxation on the shipping of Ontario. If, however, you insert the word "Ontario" as the hon. gentleman suggests, you will be levying a tax on the shipping of that province, and I am inclined to think that is beyond our poweT at the moment. Parliament can make the change in a more roundabout way, but I think the point taken by the President of the Privy Council-that if you insert the word "Ontario" in the resolution you are running up against a

well understood usage requiring a recommendation from the Crown-is quite correct.
Leaving that point, however, I want to commend, if I may, to the careful consideration of the Government-if not at this time at a more convenient moment, but at all events for inquiry-the suggestion of /ny hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) in respect to providing a hospital ship. I do not suggest that by any means as a substitute for the usual shore treatment of .sailors but as a supplement to it. I think there is such a service established- for British seamen in the North Sea; and in recent years we have seen the inauguration of a hospital ship along the Labrador coast toy Dr. Grenfell, of whose splendid services we have all heard with very great pleasure,-

That is a voluntary service. Mr.	FIELDING:-and	whose work
amongst the fishermen on the Labrador shore has been beyond all praise. It will cost a little money but our fishing business .is growing-the industry is bound to .develop to a much greater extent than it has reached at the present time-and if the minister will make inquiry into the .matter, that is all I urge at present. He .will find it quite expedient to provide a hospital ship which, could spend her time amongst our fishing fleet. At present when a man is taken ill on board a fishing vessel, that ship sacrifices time and money in making for port in order to land the sufferer for treatment. All these things cost money, and this is not the best moment to recommend the minister to expend larger sums, but- I think that in this respect the suggestion of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is a particularly good one, and I would ask the Government not to lose sight of it in the general consideration of ,this question.

I would ask the minister whether the statement made by the Shipping Federation is true or not, namely, that in some of the other ports named, the Sick Mariners' Fund has been utilized for the sick poor?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My information from the officers of the department is that that statement is not correct, but I shall have it looked into carefully.

The suggestion I would make to the hon. minister to cover the ease which I have been pressing on his attention would be to amend subsection (a) to make it read:

^ That the minister, -with the approval of the Governor in Council, may subsidize, build, rent and equip and maintain premises for hospitals for the care and treatment of sick mariners,-
and so on. That would enable the minister to expend the money collected from ships for the purpose of providing a hospital where no hospital exists at the moment, and to my mind that is one of the prime needs in connection with this matter.
I do not sympathize very much with the proposal of the Shipping Federation. I think a tax ought to be paid by shipowners for looking after sick mariners, and 1 think the large ships ought to bear the largest share of the tax because they can better afford to do so. One and one-half cents a ton is a mere bagatelle on the tonnage of even a large ship, -and it is so insignificant in the case of the smaller ships that it is hardly worth collecting. Why should not fishing vessels pay a tax; why should it be optional in their case? I think their owners should take the same responsibility with regard to their seamen as do the owners of other vessels, and I am quite sure that they are willing to bear their share. A fishing vessel of 100 tons-and that is the average size-would have to pay only $2 for one assessment, and if it paid that assessment three times a year the total sum represents very cheap insurance. A fishing vessel of that size has probably 15 to 18 sailors aboard, .and by the payment of that small premium of $6 the owners have the assurance that their men will be treated in the ports where they happen to fall sick, and altogether it is a very favourable arrangement. I think the minister would be well-advised if he so amended the Bill that fishing vessels would have to pay this duty. Then of course it would be necessary to make reasonable provision- for the sailors.
I wish to assist the minister if I can, in making this Bill a good Bill and in improving the service; therefore I would ask him to take these suggestions under favourable consideration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My present impression
is that the Bill which will be introduced following the adoption of this resolution is broad enough to cover the matter which my hon. friend has mentioned. But the whole scope of the clause can be considered when we get in committee on the Bill.

One matter was mentioned by the hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie) which pertains to the Department of Health more particularly than anything else touched upon in connection

wil-h this resolution, and that is the quality-of the drinking water supplied to sailors. He has told us that epidemics of typhoid have occurred among our seamen when as many as 75 per cent were incapacitated, due entirely to drinking contaminated water. I would ask the minister to inquire into this matter and punish people for supplying such contaminated water.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We already have that
power under the Health Act passed last session, and that particular matter is now engaging the attention of the officers of the department. There is no doubt as to the importance of insuring a supply of pure water to our sailors.
Resolution reported.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (Minister of Health) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 127 to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Sick and Distressed Mariners) .
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have been requested to let clause 32 stand. I am still considering some amendments to it which have not yet been put in definite shape. I therefore move that the clause stand and that the committee proceed to the consideration of clause 37.
Is clause 32 to be taken up later in the day?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If we have time.
* Motion agreed to.
On section 37-Proclamation by returning officer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this clause was last before the committee it had been considerably amended; several amendments had been adopted, and one amendment moved by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) was under consideration. He had moved [DOT] to strike out in lines 26, 27 and 28 on page 26 of the Bill the following words: "In every electoral district in the province of Quebec and Manitoba and in the English language only in other electoral districts."
Shall the amendment carry?

In view of the situation
as presented when the matter was p.e-viously under discussion, it seems to me that it would be fair to provide that in electoral districts where a considerable proportion of the electors cannot read English the proclamation should be published both in English and the language which these people can read and understand.

I am glad to hear the
remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Loggie). When this matter was last under consideration I suggested that the Chief Electoral Officer could instruct the returning officers in all districts where there is a considerable French population to have the proclamations and notices in those districts issued in both languages. I hope that the Acting Solicitor General has given consideration to this suggestion. In this respect the Chief Electoral Officer could be guided by this last decennial census.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
(Mr. Turgeon) explain the purpose of his proposed amendment? There would seem to he some mistake in the drafting of it.

My intention in moving the amendment was to provide that the notices and proclamations issued under this Act may be printed in French and in English not only in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, but also in all the other provinces. When T made some remarks on this subject on a previous occasion I stated that the publication of these notices in French in districts where there was no French population would not be necessary. In British Columbia, where there is no group of French-speaking people that I know of, it would not be necessary to have these notices issued in the French language. The same applies to Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan; in any parts of

these provinces where there are no Frencli people, the Fiench language need not be used. In New Brunswick we have districts which are largely peopled by French Canadians. In the northern part of the province there are five large counties the majority of the .people in which are French. According to the census of 1911, twenty-five per cent of the population of Northumberland county was made no of French-speaking people. The French population in that county is increasing more than the English population. In such districts as these I would require that both languages be employed. French people are sentimental; they appreciate anything that is done in their behalf, and nothing but good can result from a provision that these notices and proclamations may be printed in the French language. During the course of the discussion on this clause the member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis) expressed his approval of the request which I was making.
I hope, for the reasons which I have given, that the minister will be inclined to favour my amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The effect of my hon.
friend's amendment will be to strike out the words:
In every electoral district in the provinces ot Quebec and Manitoba and in the English language only in the other electoral districts.
If these words were struck out the clause would then read:
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officer shall, by a proclamation in form T., issue under his hand in the English and French languages, and shall mail one copy at least to the various postmasters of the post offices within his electoral district.
That would mean, of course, that that system would prevail throughout all the electoral districts in Canada. (Now, if I understand aright the remarks of my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) he does not intend that his amendment shall have such a wide application. When this clause was before the House on a previous occasion I was very imuch impressed by arguments which were presented in favour of some relaxation, at all events in the law as respects the printing of proclamations in the French and English languages. But practically all the arguments that can be used in favour of the printing of proclamations in French are equally applicable to the question of other languages in other parts of Canada.
Mr. d'ANJOU:	No.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend says no. But I am informed that in the northwestern portions of Canada we have large territories where no French is spoken but where many other European languages are spoken.
I know that in the portion of Canada where I reside it would be a convenience to a large number of people if the proclamations were issued in Italian; very few people there would be accommodated if the proclamations were issued in French. Unfortunately, very few of the people in my constituency can either speak or read the French language. That is to be regretted, but it would be a convenience to a good many people if these proclamations were issued in Italian, and to a number if they were issued in German. Therefore, my hon. friend will see that we are opening up a pretty wide subject if we depart from the old established section which has been in the statute book for many years. The provision of our law for many years has been the provision which appears in the clause as drafted in the Bill, namely, that in the province of Quebec and in the province of Manitoba proclamations shall be issued in both languages. After having given this matter the very best consideration that I can bestow upon it, I think at the present time it would be unwise to extend the scope of this section. Personally, this is not a matter which appeals to me very strongly; I am in no way prejudiced against the extension of the proclamation in the French language, but I know other people are; I know there are people who look upon the matter as a matter of constitutional right. Consequently the law that has been efficient and satisfactory during the past thirty or forty years should not be interfered with unless for very grave reasons, unless some very serious injustice or inconvenience has resulted from it. If a case of that kind were made out, speaking for myself, I would not hesitate to make the change; but after considering the matter -for several days and discussing it pretty generally, I think the committee would do well to allow the clause to remain as it is. There is a legal right; there is, I believe, a constitutional authority for the language of the present clause. I do not say that we have not constitutional authority to extend it, but I know we raise serious constitutional questions when we attempt to extend it. I see no great points to be gained by interfering with the present clause, and a good deal of difficulty may arise if we make the attempt. For these reasons I prefer to

stand by the section under which we have had many years of experience and which has not, so far as I know, resulted in any great inconvenience. I therefore think the amendment, while in form it is objectionable in any case and does not carry out the intention of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), should be rejected by the committee.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.

speechtext: The House again resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering clause 37, to which Mr. Turgeon had moved an amendment to strike out the following words in lines 26, 27 and 28 of page 26 of the Bill, "in every electoral district in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, and in the English language only in other electoral districts."

I took the floor before six, after the Acting Solicitor General had explained that it was impossible from his point of view to accept my amendment, with the intention of giving a further explanation as to my attitude in this matter. I admit that opinion may be divided as to the French language having equal rights with the English in Canada. I am not a lawyer-
Mr. /McMASTEtR: The father of a lawyer.

I am the father of a lawyer, it is true. Though I am not a constitutional authority, I have my convictions on matters affecting the constitution. I was born into life, I might say, on the discussion of a constitutional point. I came into New Brunswick at the time of the school troubles and the assertion by a portion of the people of that province of what they believed to be their constitutional
rights. After the Privy Council had declared that New Brunswick had no constitutional right to separate schools, I was the first to call on my people in the northern part of the province not to press the agitation further, but to accept any amendment which might be granted by the Provincial Government, rather than cause the least trouble. My admiration for the constitution has not decreased since then. I admire the constitution, because I have suffered for it. I would be the last man in Canada to ask for an amendment to the constitution, believing that one amendment might weaken the whole structure. The British North America Act is a tree, carrying in its growth the elements of the bounteous soil, and the tree has grown as the country has grown in population and developed. The Act itself carries an acknowledgment of what I aim saying, because French w>as conceded in the province of Manitoba when at that time there was a certain French population as a result of *an exodus from the province of Quebec. There were no French at all, however, at that time in Saskatchewan and Alberta. In New Brunswick the increase of population since Confederation is due to the French who have remained at home cherishing the soil of their forefathers.
I am asking by this amendment that the French language be recognized in every Federal record, as has been so eloquently and clearly demonstrated by hon. members on this side of the House particularly my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) and my hon. friend (Mr. Beland) who have spoken on the amendment. The Acting Solicitor General says that if he accepted the amendment, he would have to accede also to requests for the same privileges in regard to other languages spoken in this country. Personally I would not object to any group of people in this country speaking neither English or French, being given the privilege of having these documents printed in their own language, in order that they might better be able to comprehend them and make themselves acquainted with the principles upon which they are to pronounce themselves. In a mixed country like Canada we should be ready to grant concessions to accommodate our peoples. We know that there are languages in this country which have not the rights which the French language has in Canada, and I leave it to the Government or the minister who is in charge of this Bill to introduce such an amendment if he so desires.

As I said before six o'clock, I want to be practical. I am not moving my amendment as a matter of pride or jealousy. I want these documents to be published only in districts where there is a group of French people to read and ponder over them. I do not see why any hon. member on the other side of the House should not accede to this amendment. I am glad to see the Acting Prime Minister in his seat. He was not present when I spoke on this question a few days ago, and again this afternoon. I believe that if there is one Canadian who has given authority to my understanding of the rights of the French language in Canada, and has contributed to the harmonious feeling which such recognition may create, more particularly under present conditions, it is my right hon. friend, the Acting Prime Minister. At the opening of the session he delivered a most eloquent speech in French, delivered it more eloquently than could I. He spoke like a master of the language. He has given ah example of admiration of the rights of the constitution, and his action tends effectively to create further harmony in the country. I believe that if I had not been prompted by the effect that speech of the right hon. gentleman created upon my mind I would not have brought in this amendment. The Confederation has grown in fifty years, it has developed, and its- privileges have been extended to every territory it covers. Therefore, I believe that the House will be prepared to accept my amendment. But, I want to be practical in this matter. 1 would be willing that my amendment, as worded, should be altered in a certain way to meet all practical needs while at the same time maintaining the principle upon which it is based. In that case I might suggest a change in the phraseology to the Acting Solicitor General instead of insisting upon the wording as. it is there. I do not withdraw my amendment, but I would be willing to change it so that it would read in this way:
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officer shall, by proclamation, in form L,, issued under his hand in the English and French languages, in [DOT] every electoral district in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba and in such other electoral districts of other provinces as the Chief Electoral Officer will deem it advisable to so direct, and in the English language only in the other electoral districts, and mailed one copy of each to the various postmasters of the post offices within his electoral district.
And so on. I move my amendment with the explanation which I gave this afternoon. I believe that this House will have no
good ground to refuse to accept the amendment which, under the circumstances, can only bring about good in the future.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. member to say that he withdraws his amendment and that he substitutes this amendment for it?

I do not intend to withdraw it yet, but I want to substitute these words. The effect will be that the proclamation will be issued in the French language in any district where the Electoral Officer himself considers that it would be warranted by the number of French people in that district. I do not say where these districts should be; I leave that to the judgment of the electoral officer.

Mr. Chairman, I felt very sorry when I heard the hon. the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie)foefore dinner state that it would be impossible for him to consent to this amendment to the Act. The reasons which he advanced were not acceptable to me and in reply to the hon. gentleman I will give a few reasons why this amendment should be accepted. The law has been such that during the last thirty or forty years there has been only two provinces in which regulations and proclamations have of necessity been printed in the English and French languages. The Fathers of Confederation agreed that- both the English and French languages should be official languages in this country. The use of either. language has been the right of any member ini the House of Commons since Confederation. In the Senate Chamber to-day we witnessed the ceremony of assenting to Bills which had been passed by this House, and before the deputy of His Excellency the Governor General these Bills were assented to in both the French and English languages. The minister said that he could not see his way clear to the acceptance of this amendment, that it would open the door to lots of trouble, but I would say to him that I can foresee no trouble that would foe caused by the use of these two official languages in carrying on elections in this country. I am not speaking about any other language; I am only speaking about the two official languages. Therefore, I cannot agree with him when he says that the adoption of this proposition will open the door to trouble in the future. Another argument that has been advanced is that this has never been done 'before. If it has never been done before it is no reason why it should not be done now. We are making a new Act and we are only asking for what is within our rights.

We are not asking for any favours, only our rights, and therefore I cannot see why the minister should not accept the amendment and allow the minority the right which was granted to them by the Fathers of Confederation. The fact is that the recognition of these two official languages was one of the foundation stones of Confederation. There must be some reason with which we have not been acquainted that prevents the acceptance of this proposition. We have no claim from any other nationality to have these proclamations published in their language. We have only two official languages and it is only these languages that are referred to in this amendment. I ask that the Maritime Provinces be placed on the same footing as any other province in Canada, that recognition be given to their rights, and in doing that I feel that I am only asking something which they should receive at the hands of this Government.

Is the hon. member
trying-
Order.
Is the hon. gentleman claiming that the law should be changed?
We are making the law now.

We are not asking that the law be changed at all; we are only asking that the law enacted at the time of Confederation be continued. The question may be asked: "Why did you not ask this before?" Well, there are many things as to which the same question might be asked. The country is growing and the French population is growing in numbers also- the French population throughout the Maritime Provinces has been considerably augmented. There is nothing wrong about the request we are making; it is simply that the election proclamation and the various election documents be printed in French. I do not consider that we are making any extraordinary request in asking for that and I shall be pleased at any time to meet my constituents and justify the stand I am taking to-night. I believe they will endorse that stand because I know them and they know me. The majority in my province are generous and I am asking the majority in this House to be equally so. When the English people in my county ask for anything that is reasonable the French people cheerfully grant it. I am now making a reasonable request to hon. members who form the majority in this House and who represent the majority in
the country at large. The request that I make is that the two official languages shall be on the same footing as they are in our schools and in other institutions in that part of the country from which I come. I ask the supporters of the Government to join with us in seeing that our application is acceded to. Why not permit the French people in my province to more accurately grasp what is going on at election time when they could do that better through the medium of their own language? The franchise has been granted to women, but some of the women of my nationality in New Brunswick have not had the advantage of an English education and unless these documents are printed in French they will be handicapped to a certain extent in following the course of the elections. Let the Government grant this right and they will receive every credit from the people who will benefit by it. I again appeal to the Government to give us that justice and fair play to which we are entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If I understood my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) aright he asked that the French language be used throughout certain electoral districts in Canada to the extent of printing the proclamation and election papers in French rather as a privilege than as a right; but I gather from what the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Leger) has said that he made the claim as a right-
No.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-as a right given to the people at Confederation under the British North America Act. I am not going to labour the point, but I think it just as well to have a clear statement of the law as far as * I know it, because there are provisions in the Act which will clear up any misunderstanding which may exist. The only clause in the British North America Act, to my knowledge, that bears upon the question is section 133 which reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the Debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the Legislature of Quebec,_
I think the committee will agree with me that that clause does not refer to these election documents or proclamations. The next clause is:
and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses;
Now I sbumit that the election proclamations are neither "records" nor "journals"

"of these Houses". The third clause is worded thus:
-and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this Act and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
That is the third clause and I think it is clear beyond doubt that it could have no application to the question under discussion. The next and last clause is:
The Acts of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
I think. Mr. Chairman, it is equally clear that the last clause has no application whatever to the subject under discussion, viz: The right that was granted to the people of the country under the British North America Act; and I merely point out to my hon. friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger) that in my humble opinion that does not include the election documents as set out in clause 37 of the Bill under discussion. There is another enactment, relating to the province of Manitoba, which I had better put on Hansard at the same time. That is to be found in the Manitoba Act, passed in the year 1870' when Manitoba entered Confederation. Paragraph 23 of that Act provides as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the Debates of the Houses of the Legislature, and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses.
That is the first clause of the section of the Manitoba Act bearing upon the question.
That paragraph can have no application to the section under discussion.
The next paragraph is:
And either of those languages may be used by any person, or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under the British North America Act, 186", or in or from all or any of the courts of the province.
The second paragraph, you will see, Mr. Chairman, can have no application to the subject under discussion.
The last paragraph of the section is:
The Acts of the Legislature shall be printed and published in both of these languages.
Now, I submit that under a strict reading of the'Manitoba Act it is very doubtful if there is any obligation upon this Parliament to print in the French language in the Province of Manitoba any documents relating to elections. That, however, has

been established through long years of practice, and the Government has no intention of departing from what we look upon as an established practice-Whether established strictly in accordance with law or for what other reason I cannot say at this time. I am pointing this out for the purpose of showing my hon. friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger) that so far as I am aware the request that he makes is not founded in right; it must be viewed as a matter of privilege. He is quite within his right in asking for it, and I am quite sure that this Parliament has full power and authority to grant it if it sees fit. But in the present Bill we do not go as far as that, we are merely leaving the law and practice where it has been for many years, and I have yet to hear that it has caused any great degree of inconvenience in any part of the country.

May I ask my hon. friend a question before he proceeds further? What kind of a document in his opinion is the Canada Gazette? Is it a "Journal" of the House; is it a "record" of the House; is it an Act of Parliament? Still, it is published in tooth languages all over the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that when we
come down to examine that question strictly, it may be found that the Canada Gazette is published in both languages as a matter of convenience. It is nearer an approach to a record of the House or to a statute, because it does contain all our Orders in Council, which have the same force and effect as statutes of this Parliament. In a word, in my humble opinion, it is a nearer approach to the records of the House than any election document.
In what way may I ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Simply because it is a record of the legislative enactments of this House, whether carried out by statute or by Order in Council. It is a resume of the powers this Parliament has exercised, whether sitting as Parliament or whether sitting as the executive authority, as the Governor in Council. Therefore I say it more nearly approaches the language of the British North America Act than any election document could. I think that perhaps on a strict examination of the section it might fairly be held that the Canada Gazette need not be published in the French language. I would not advocate such a thing; I would advocate its continued publication in both languages. But when one interprets a statute one is bound to interpret it strictly, and I doubt very much

whether on a strict interpretation the Canada Gazette would he held to he a record or "journal" of this House, although it very nearly approaches it.

The British North America Act as explained by the minister does not inention a word in reference to the proclamation for elections being printed in tooth languages either in Manitoba or in the Province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.

Now, is not the law of
this House the law which was established after Confederation, and which law was made to meet the requirements of that day? The official languages were established by the British North America Act, and then this House has gone so far as to say: We are going to allow proclamations for elections in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba to be printed in the two languages. If such be the case, and the two official languages were established by the Confederation Act, we are only asking now for an extension of the Act wherever it is needed, whether in the province of New Brunswick, of Nova Beotia, of Prince Edward Island or df Ontario. I never contended that the British North America Act went so far as to say that these proclamations should be printed in French and in English in Quebec and Manitoba; that is not what I meant. But I believe I am right in my contention that the law in regard to the use of the two official languages as laid down in the British North America Act may be extended when it is deemed desirable to do so. I would like to have an explanation from the hon. minister as to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It may be that I misunderstood my hon. friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger) because I certainly heard him repeat on two or three occasions that the use of the French language as described by him was a matter of right established by the Constitution at the time of Confederation, and my only object in rising was to point out to him the exact terms of the section.
Does the Bill provide for the text of the proclamation to be issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
It does. This Bill could not be read a second time before it was printed in both languages?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the fact.

Then why should not
the proclamation be published all over
Canada in both languages, if it is part of a Bill adopted by this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A Bill is published in both languages in accordance with the requirements of the Constitution and as an act of this House, and this Bill will be published in both languages. There our duty ceases. There is no requirement outside the province of Quebec that election documents shall be printed in French. Now, I may not know all the legislation dealing with this subject, and I want to guard myself to this extent, that there may be some other Act of which I am not aware with regard to the printing in French of the Canada Gazette or some other document. I am referring only to the law that was passed at the time of Confederation, because that was the point raised by my hon. friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger). I am not expressing my own opinion as to the propriety of using the French language more freely than we have used it in the past. What I say is, that, viewing the matter from all points, having regard to the records of the past, and having regard also to the fact that no great inconvenience has ever been suffered, I think our safest, wisest and fairest course is to adopt the clause as printed in the Bill.

I do not share the views of my friend from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger) and I take issue with the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie). I claim that the word " records" used in section 133 includes everything that is kept in the custody of any official of this House. I go further and say that when T ask for a return in this House, that return is a "record " of the House, and if I wanted to insist on the strict interpretation of clause 133 I would have a right to see that that record was deposited on the table of the House in both languages. Section 133 does not say " may," it says " shallit is not permissive, it is imperative.
Now, Sir, what is a " record?" A record, according to Murray's New English Dictionary, is:
The fact or attribute of being so; having been committed by writing as authentic evidence of a matter having a legal importance;-
Now, where is the evidence that the election was held, that is, that the proclamation was issued therefor?
as evidence of the proceedings or verdict of a court of justice; evidence which is thus preserved and may be appealed to in case of dispute.
[DOT]2274

What are these election papers, and what does the Act say about them? These election papers are issued under the order of the highest court in this country, the Parliament of Canada; and for the purpose of making sure that they shall be issued Parliament appoints a Chief Electoral Officer. The Chief Electoral Officer is vested with quasi-judicial powers; he has to see that this law is carried out according to the terms which Parliament has enacted. The definition of " record " as given by Murray is this:	" Evidence which is
preserved and may be appealed to in case of dispute." Section 75 of this Bill provides :
The Chief Electoral Officer shall, subject to the provisions of this Act. retain in his possession the papers transmitted to him by any returning officer,-
These papers are the election papers, and they are defined in the Interpretation Act. The section continues:
-with the return, for at least one year-
Nobody will dispute that for that year these papers which are in the custody of the Chief Electoral Officer are "records" of this House. If they are not, I do not know what they are.
__if the election is not contested during that
time, and, if the election is contested, then for one year after the termination of such contestation.
If the election is contested there is the evidence, which is kept to be used before the court in a determination of the case. The only evidence that the election has been held is the proclamation which says that on such a day, toy order of the Governor in Council, an election shall be held. I submit, therefore, that all these papers become records of this House and ought to be kept as such. If you want evidence of the fact that those who first drafted this law had the same idea as I have, take the wording of this Bill. Section 37 reads*
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officer shall, by a proclamation in form L, issued under his hand in the English and French languages in every electoral district in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, and In the English language only-
What is the word "only" there for? If the contention of my hon. friends is right that the only official language in which this proclamation should be issued is the English language, why use the word "only?" That word was put in because those who were drafting the clause were giving to section 133 of the British North America Act the same interpretation that I am giving to

it to-night. If what my hon. friends contend was so clear in the minds of those who drafted the clause, all they had to say was that the proclamation should be issued in both the French and the English languages in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, and stop there. But, as I say, their interpretation of section 133 was the same as mine.
Now, my hon. friend says that "record' does not mean these election papers; that what is and what is not to be considered a record is a matter to be interpreted by the courts. I contend that all papers which come into the custody or under the care of any officer of this House become "records" of the House if they are kept for a purpose. When these election papers go into the custody of the Chief Electoral Officer they are records in the custody of an officer of this House. If the election is contested he has to keep these papers one year after the proceedings in the contestation are ended. Why? Because these documents are to be used as evidence before a court of justice. I refer again to Murray's definition of "record" as "evidence which is preserved and may be appealed to in case of dispute.
If these papers are not to be "appealed to in case of dispute," why preserve them? The only use to which they can be put is to determine whether or not, when the election took place, everything was properly done. When there is a recount, from whom do you get the ballots and the papers? From the same officer. "Election papers" means all those documents which were used in an election. The strict interpretation of this clause, therefore, being that all documents used in a federal election become records of this House, it is imperative that they be printed in the official language of this country, which is a dual language, English and French, and they stand on a par. Statutes are not enacted for the purpose of throwing ink on a sheet of paper; they are supposed to mean something. If publication of these papers has been restricted in the other provinces to the English language, that restriction is an infringement of existing Tights. According to the Interpretation Act, Revised Statutes, the word "shall" is used-it is not permissive; it is imperative. In section 37, therefore, there is a command to print these notices in both languages in the two provinces mentioned and in English only in the other provinces.
Air. AlORPHY: The hon. gentleman says that the Chief Electoral Officer is bound under section 75 to keep the election papers in his possession for a year, and in case

of contested election for a further year from the termination of the contestation. Now, what does the Chief Electoral Officer do with them after that? '
Does my hon. friend mean to say that the question whether a paper is a "record" depends upon whether it is preserved in perpetuity?
I simply ask the question.

He destroys them, I suppose. Does my hon. friend contend that a printed Bill used in this House is not a "record," even though it is of no further use'when it is merged into a statute? I say that the question whether a paper is a "record" does not depend on how long it is preserved. If a paper comes into the possession of an officer of this House for a purpose, in order that it may toe used as evidence in a court of justice or anywhere else, it becomes a "record" of this House, and under section 133 of the British North America Act it is imperative that it be printed in both languages. I make this point, not for tihe purpose of claiming anything, but for the purpose of showing my hon. friends opposite, \vho think they are always giving us privileges when under the constitution we have rights, that we are not here asking ifor privileges. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) has been ,moved in the best interest of the people pf Canada. I understand my hon. friends to answer our argument by saying: Why pot print the proclamation in Russian, in polish? I have more respect for the constitution than that. When the constitution states that 'the official language of this country shall be dual, that does not mean a dozen or eighteen languages. It is no use trying to get out of the difficulty in that iway. The language of Canada is dual; I do not say [which language is "the" language. There is but one official language in this country, and it is English and French, or if you like to reverse the two, French and English,-because the French language was here 'before the English language was. I say this, because the other pight the hon. member ifor Perth North (Mr. Morphy) said: When you give an inch to those fellows, they want an ell.
. Mr. MORPHY: No, a mile.

Well, that is just like my hon. friend. That was beyond his vision, and he always looks beyond his vision when he makes Tash statements like that. We are not asking for any privileges; we 145
have always been giving in, giving in, and giving in. As I said just now, according to this section, there are many documents that come down to this House, and if we ,were to sit-
Tight.

No, but to sit still on our rights, we could delay the proceedings of this House. There is a rule in this House that says that before a Bill can be read the .second time, it shall be printed in both French and English. Time and again, we fiave refrained from insisting on that, because every hon. member on this side understands English, and when it came to a matter, of expediting business we all agreed not to insist on a Bill being printed in French. But I do not want the country to remain under the impression that the statement made in this House by my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) is true. There is not a discussion in this House on which We do not hold different opinions because "tot capita, tot sensus." There may ibe a thousand different interpretations that can be given to that section of the statute. But if my hon. friends opposite are sincere, I will make a proposition to them, and we shall settle the question once and for all. If my hon. friends opposite think that they are right and that this means that the proclamations and other documents should lbe printed in the English language only, I will ask them to accept this amendment. Let .the clause read as follows:
Within two days after the receipt of the writ of election the returning officer shall, by a proclamation in form L, issued under his hand, and mailed one copy at least to the various postmasters of the post offices within his electoral district, indicate-
Drop out the words "in the English and French languages in every electoral district in 'the provinces of Quebec and Mani-,toba, and in the English language only in other electoral districts," and we shall go to the highest tribunal in the land and find out what section 133 of the 'constitution means. If my hon. friends opposite are willing to accept that amendment, I think the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) and the hon. member for Kent, N.B., (Mr. Leger) will be satisfied. There is the test.

Does the hon. member take the ground that it is necessary, according to the constitution, that these proclamations shall-he laid great emphasis on the word "shall"-be published in the English and French languages in all parts of this country?



. Mr. BUREAU: The section as it stands [DOT]says in so many words that the proclamations shall be printed in English and French in two provinces, namely, in Quebec and Manitoba, and then it says "and in English only in the other provinces." No other interpretation can be given to that than that Quebec and Manitoba are the only two provinces under the Act as it stands in which the proclamations have to be printed in English and French, because we have a right to determine these things. We may legislate ourselves ou't of certain rights if we want to do so; that is the privilege of a Parliament. But what I say is this. Drop out the words "in English and French in Quebec and Manitoba and in English only in the other provinces," and let the clause go at that, and publish the proclamations in English only. Then the courts will determine the matter.

I think any hon. friend misunderstood my question. I asked him if he takes the ground that, according to the British North America Act, it is absolutely necessary that these proclamations in all parts of the Dominion shall foe published in both languages.

I say that the British North America Act uses the word "shall." These election papers are a "record" of this House when they are returned to the Chief Electoral Officer, and the word "shall," according to the Interpretation Act, is imperative and not permissive. In other words, I say that if a man wanted to insist, if this clause did not read as it does to-day-if the words "in Etaglish and French in Manitoba and Quebec and in English only in the other provinces" were left out- he could compel the Chief Electoral Officer to print in every part of Canada, these proclamations in both the English and the French languages.
My hon. friend's position is entirely illogical.
Oh, no.
I say that it is, if he takes the ground that the proclamation must be published in both languages throughout the Dominion.
My hon. friend does not understand me.
Probably not.

I am not discussing the clause as it stands to-day before the House. Clause 37 is a re-enactment of the section as it existed before-so I am informed by
