the Acting Solicitor General. That clause determines in what provinces the proclamation shall be printed in both languages. There are two such provinces in the Dominion of Canada-Quebec and Manitoba. The clause goes further. I will read it to my hon. friend.
Air. GLASS; I want what the British North America Act says.

I told my hon. friend that we could legislate ourselves out of certain rights and privileges if we wanted to. Parliament is free to say that those proclamations shall be printed in English or in French only in any part of Canada. But I say: If you are sincere, if you want to test the matter, drop out those words entirely from the clause, and then if anybody is dissatisfied, we shall go before the courts and have the matter determined and an interpretation given to this clause. Aly hon. friend need not laugh and shrug his shoulders. He knows very well, if we came to argue that point and have it determined by the court, what election papers constitute when they are in the hands of the Chief Electoral Officer. I could have the court determine that they become "records" when they are in the hands of the Chief Electoral Officer for a month or a year; and as long as they are "records" for any time at all they must follow the general rule to which records are submitted when they are records of this House. I said that I wanted to make myself clear on this point, because I do not want the hon. member for Perth North (Mr. Morphy) and some of his confreres to believe we are begging favours from them and to let 9 p.m. the country believe they are unwilling to grant favours. This is a right, and there is a way of testing that. Leave those words out of the clause; then let the proclamation be published in the French language only, if you like, or in the English language only, if you like, and let the people who feel aggrieved on account of such proclamation go before the courts and have the matter determined once and for all.

I realize that the question under discussion is not only one of great importance but one of a very delicate character, which we should all approach with a most sincere desire to find a ground of agreement. It is a question upon which many of our people hold very strong convictions. It is a question upon which perhaps a great many of our people have very strong prejudices, and these convictions

and these prejudices do often come into conflict. Just how far the French language is an official language in Canada is unhappily the subject of debate. Up to a certain point there is no question whatever. My hon. friends who have spoken before have indicated the point up to which there is no debate. There is no question that the French language is the language of this Parliament on equal terms with the English language. It is so in the Senate, it is so in the House of Commons, it is so in the province of Quebec, it is so, as the Acts have indicated, in the province of Manitoba. Up to that point there is no dispute. We all agree that as respects this Parliament and the legislature of Quebec and the legislature of Manitoba, the French and English languages stand on equal temis. The moment you pass beyond that, you get into the field of debate, and when hon. gentlemen who feel strongly on what I might call the French side assert that the French language stands equal with the English throughout the Dominion, they run to a point which is immediately resisted by a great many people. I am not trying to determine the question myself, but I do want us to clearly understand that- beyond that certain point, beyond the point of the legislatures of Quebec and Manitoba, and this Parliament, it is not a clear question. At all events, it is a question that always has been and I suppose always will be, in dispute. The records of this Parliament, we are told, are to be printed in French. The hon. member for Three Rivers has just put up what seems to me, as a layman, to be a pretty good interpretation of what the " records " should mean. It is a new view of the matter to me. I do not know whether it has been presented before. It is 'rather a curious fact that for fifty-odd years we have been viewing it in another way. If the question came before the Supreme Court, it is possible the view of my hon. friend would prevail, but that is a purely legal question on which I as a layman would not presume to express an opinion.
I prefer to consider the matter from the point of view of what I might call public convenience, mutual convenience, a desire to meet each other, if we can, on all these matters, to respect each other's convictions-aye, and sometimes to respect each other's prejudices when they are based upon convictions. If I look upon this matter entirely from the point of view of my constituents and my province, I want no change in the law as it now stands. So far as they are concerned, I am content with the clause as it stands in the Act. But if 145J
in another province some of my brother members find themselves embarrassed and in difficulty, I would like to be mindful of their troubles and not be so selfish as to think of only my own. Down in Nova Scotia we have a large French population, and I am glad to say that we have practically no language trouble whatever. We have adapted our school system, as far as possible, to the needs of our French-speaking people, and the result is that, every Frenchman, I believe, in the whole province of Nova Scotia understands and speaks both languages. We rejoice that it is so, and on behalf of the French-speaking people of Nova Scotia I would not desire any change whatever.
But my hon. friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Turgeon) says that they have difficulties in his province and he would like to meet them. If the object of his amendment is simply to provide a proclamation in French for those who cannot read English, if it is a practical question, then I am heartily with him. I sympathize largely with his object, but I do not quite like the words in which he has drawn his amendment. He proposes to leave it to be determined by the Chief Electoral Officer sitting in Ottawa as to the cases, other than those specified in the Aet, in which a proclamation in French shall be issued. I do not like that provision. I do not think the Chief Electoral Officer sitting here in Ottawa is the officer best qualified to know the conditions with regard to language in all parts of Canada. I do not think it is very practical. I am not going to move any amendment, because it is too delicate and serious a matter to plunge into amendments. I am simply going to offer a suggestion to the minister which is in line with that of the hon. member for Gloucester to a certain extent and in line with what I understood my hon. friend from Northumberland to suggest, although he made no motion. My point is that if there is any community in Canada where the people do not understand the English language, I do not care in what province it is, I am willing to give them a proclamation in French. I am not willing to give it to them in Italian, I am not willing to give it to them in German. I am not scared by this idea that if we do this for our French friends we must do it for all other nations; the French language does not stand in Canada on an equal footing with the Italian or the German, it has, within certain limits, a clear and distinct position, and within those limits I would like to stand by and support my hon. friends-when they go

beyond that and want something else, perhaps I cannot agree with them. I am not prepared to say that the Italian, or the German, or the Scandinavian, or any other man of foreign birth who comes to-Canada has the same language rights in Canada as our French friends. The French language has a certain established right in Canada, and I am willing that that be recognized and given even beyond strictly what the law proposes.
I have said that in the province of Nova Scotia we have a large French population. In the western part of Nova Scotia, in Yarmouth county, and in the neighbouring county of Digby, there is a large French population. Coming east to Halifax county, in the eastern part, there is a considerable French population. Passing further east, in the county of Antigonish, in the county of Inverness, in the county of Richmond, and in fact in quite a number of the districts of Nova Scotia, there is a large French-speaking population. But inasmuch as they all understand and speak the English language, as they have never made any demand whatever to have these documents published in French, I do not want any proceedings to be taken to publish the proclamation in French with the view of obliging anybody down there. The French-speaking people of Nova Scotia do not need it, they do not want it, they have never asked for it. But if there are in New Brunswick or any other province substantial groups of people speaking the French language and not understanding English, I say that in that case I would give the returning officer the right to decide to publish the proclamation there in French;-no, not the right to decide: if he has knowledge that there is a substantial group of French-speaking people in an electoral district who do not understand English, and will not understand the proclamation if published in English, then it should be his duty to publish the proclamation both in French and in English. With that object in view I am going, not to make a motion, for the matter is too serious to rush into motions, but to offer this for the consideration of my hon. friend from Gloucester, because I think it is his idea, and to ask the minister to give it due consideration. I would not alter the clause as it stands, but I would put in this proviso at the end: " Provided, however, that in any electoral district in which, to the knowledge of the returning officer, there is a considerable number of electors who are familiar with the French language but do not under-
stand the English language, the proclamation shall be issued in both languages."

In offering a few remarks on this clause I may say that in clear recognition of the principle involved in it, my first intention was to speak in French, but I realize that by so doing I would place some of my hon. friends opposite in precisely the same position in which they want to place the French-speaking electors of New Brunswick. For this reason, therefore, and for the cause of good understanding, I will strive to offer my remarks in English. The minister asked a moment ago if we were asking for the recognition of a right. I must say that personally I have been very much impressed by the case made by my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). I listened to the reading of the clause by the minister and I think he has well demonstrated that election documents constitute properly "records" of the House and as such come within clause 133. If you turn to page 86 of this Bill yo.u will find Form L which is a:
Proclamation of the returning officer declaring time and place fixed for the nomination of candidates, and the day for opening the poll.
I understand this form has been translated and constitutes a part of the French translation of the Bill. I submit that these same proclamations come within clause 133 for these reasons: First,, because they are records of Parliament and also because they are part of an Act of Parliament. I would go further. I think that we on this side of the House have shown large tolerance. We have been suggesting different ways out of the difficulty. My hon. friend from Gloucester was ready to leave it to the Chief Electoral Officer to decide in which constituencies these proclamations should be translated. My hon. friend from Three Rivers was perfectly willing to leave it to the courts to decide. And now we have another suggestion from my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) who, if I understand him aright, wants merely to put a proviso at the end of the clause in order to cover the case of constituencies where a large portion of the population is French. Any of these suggestions, if the minister will accept it, will meet with our views.
What we do object to is to leave in an Act of the Parliament of Canada a provision that these proclamations may be issued in English only in other electoral districts which means all electoral districts outside of Quebec and Manitoba leaving out those portions of New Brunswick, Nova

Scotia and some parts of Ontario where a large portion of the population is French. It has been shown that in New Brunswick one-third of the population is French; it has been shown that in Ontario you hare three hundred thousand people who speak French; and it has been shown that in the Maritime Provinces one hundred and eighty thousand people speak French. Under these circumstances, I submit, a large portion of the population would be deprived of the right of reading these proclamations in their own language.
I would go further and say that what we ask for is not at all cumbersome. To issue these proclamations in the two languages would not be expensive and it would be very useful. This matter receives added importance by reason of the fact that we now have the woman vote. There is a large number of eases where a man will speak both languages whereas his wife and some of his children will not because they have lived within the more restricted area of the family circle. By reason of the increased French population in some of the counties, and also by reason of the fact that women have been given the vote, it is more necessary than ever that the proclamations should be issued in these counties in both languages. It is not only a matter of dealing with the law but it is also a matter of carrying out the spirit of the law. This clause 133 has often come up for consideration in this House. I remember that when it was my pride to be a member of the press gallery I listened very often to the discussion of that clause. There are two classes of opinion as to the meaning of the clause. One is the broad school, the school of broadminded men, who consider that the recognition of the bilingual principle will be beneficial to this country and who are quite willing to apply it every time that occasion arises. There is another school of opinion, a school-I will say without hesitation-of narrow-minded men who consider the fact "that we should have two official languages in this country as a near-calamity and every time an opportunity presents itself for the application of the principle to the French language they are trying to restrict the sense of the clause to their own narrow interpretation of it. I should think that my hon. friend the minister is inclined to be of the former school because when my hon. friend from Gloucester first presented his case the minister admitted that he sympathized with the proposition and said that he would take it into consideration,
and that he hoped he would be able to come back with some amendment meeting our views. We went to bed that night with the vain hope that it would materialize. Unfortunately this clause was left over for a few days, and this afternoon the minister makes the statement that he can do nothing. He went as far as to say-I hope I am not misquoting him-I took down his words:
I am not personally prejudiced against the extension of the French language in this respect. but I know that other people are prejudiced against it.
, I think that is what the minister said this afternoon. I would like to ask him:	who are those men, who are
those members of the House who are prejudiced against the French language to such an extent that they have prevented him against his inclination, from yielding to our demand and forced him to come back here and make the statement that he could not do anything? The other day the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) put a question in this House, as follows:
Would my hon. friend raise any objection to changing this clause so as to make it compulsory for the proclamation to be printed in forty or fifty languages throughout the Western part of the country?
My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has just dealt with that side of the matter, but I would like to add this to what has been said: I understand that we have before us an electoral Bill and that in order that a man shall have the right to vote in this country he must first he naturalized. If I turn to the Naturalization Act of 1919 I find in clause 2 subsection (3) that one of the essentials to naturalization is that he is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of either the English or French language.
' I submit, Mr. Chairman, that there is not one elector in this country who can vote .unless he has been naturalized, and that there is not one elector who has been naturalized without being able to speak either French or English. Therefore, I think that the question put by my hon. friend was .altogether irrelevant.
, I have much respect for the people of this country who speak Italian or any other language that it pleases them to speak, but I think that if they are electors they are ,in good standing with our Constitution only if they speak either French or English. I do not wish to extend the discussion any further, but before I take my seat I would like to put on Hansard a few lines from an

editorial in the Montreal Star of yesterday on the bilingual question generally:
The Bilingual Canadian.
A knowledge of French-by which is not meant merely a bowing acquaintance-is a very valuable asset throughout the world. In Canada it is naturally of peculiar value. Ninety per cent of the suspicion and misunderstanding between the two groups that make up this country's population and that retard the progress and well-being of Canada is due to the inability of these groups to understand each other's mother tongue.
Whether or not compulsory French or English in our schools and universities is a wise policy, there is certainly no doubt about the wisdom of the French or English student who determines to learn the other language. He is the master of an asset which will serve and- sooner or later-pay him well. More than that, he is a better Canadian.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are not any words, they are the words of a newspaper that we have no reason to suspect of any partiality towards us. Yet it says that giving due regard and justice to both languages in this country makes one a better Canadian. I hope the .minister will resist the opposition to this clause being changed -a change which is likely to have the effect of making many of our people better Canadians-and will yield to our demand that the clause be properly amended.
Mr. EDWARD'S:	The hon. member for
Shelburne and Queen's said this was a very delicate question, and I think he repeated the word "delicate" several times, so impressed was he with the delicacy of the subject which he was discussing. The hon. gentleman to-day finds this question delicate as he found it in the past. It was too delicate a question for the hon. gentleman to deal with at all, previous to the elections of 1900, 1904, 1908, or 1911 when he was a member of the Government of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurder. And, for part of that time at least, the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was a member of that administration as Solicitor General. A great wrong was being inflicted upon certain classes ol people in this country then, and there was a great opportunity for those hon. gentlemen who were members of the Government of the day to take the necessary steps to remove these wrongs. Now, as illustrating the wrongs that were being inflicted during all those years upon certain groups of French Canadians who were settled in different parts of the country, I wish to place on record a statement made by the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in this House on the 23rd February, 1910:
To-day the sun in his daily career doeo not shed his light upon any people on the face of
[Mr. Fielding.!
the earth enjoying more liberty than my fellow-countrymen of French extraction.
That was an expression of opinion from the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier one year prior to the election of 1911, and in view of that statement there could not have been any outcry at that time front the hon. member for Three Rivers, the hon. member for tBeauce (iMr. Reland), the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, nor the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who were all members of the Liberal Government. Not one of these gentlemen at that time raised the cry that the French settlers grouped in different parts of the country were being imposed upon or were being deprived of their rights. But my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's now says it is a delicate question. Yes, too delicate for him to touch and too delicate it has been for him to touch in the past. During all the time he had the power, and the right, and the opportunity to afford redress, it was too delicate a question for him and his colleagues to have anything to do with.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that this matter may be considered from two standpoints. When it was up in the House a few days ago hon. gentlemen opposite took a somewhat different ground from what they are taking to-day. I do not think that the hon. member for Kent, N.B., took any different ground; but other hon. gentlemen on that occasion rather emphasized this point, that there were in certain parts of the country-in the constituencies of Gloucester and Kent, N.B., and other ridings down there, as well as in certain constituencies in Ontario and other provinces- groups of French Candians who suffered inconvenience or were placed at a disadvantage because they were unable to read the election proclamation as it was printed in English. The other night it was a question of inconvenience or inability on the part of these people to read the proclamation. To-night they have somewhat departed from that attitude. Now if you take the ground that the election proclamation should be printed in another language than English because of the inability of certain portions of the people to read it in English, then I contend that you must open the door to the people of other "nationalities who are resident in various parts of this country, because I find that in the province of Manitoba the Hermans and the Austrians are each more numerous than the French Canadians in that province. I also find that in the province of Saskatchewan and in the province of Alberta like-

wise, the Germans, Austrians and Scandinavians are much more numerous than the French Canadians. If then it is right to claim that the proclamation should be printed so that all the people of the country may be able to read it and thereby inform themselves as to the instructions to be given to the electors-if that is the ground you are to take, then I say your argument for having it printed in French will apply with equal force to having that document printed in German, Austrian, Scandinavian, and a great many other languages. But hon. gentlemen took a different position to-day. They assumed the position that the proclamations should be printed in the French as well as in English because the constitution conferred that right. In that connection my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's was very emphatic in stating that he would not print the proclamation in Italian, or in Austrian, or in Scandinavian, or in any of these other languages. One part of my hon. friend's argument was that there are certain French Canadians who are unable to inform themselves as to this proclamation because it is printed in a language they cannot understand; and at the same time the hon. gentleman say's he will let thousands and tens of thousands of people of other nationalities remain in ignorance so far as the election proclamation is concerned. That is the attitude which these hon. gentlemen have taken.
If my hon. friend will allow me a correction, I think he is not fair to me; I never took that attitude.
I was referring to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's.

My hon. friend spoke of hon. members on this side. If the hon. gentleman will refer to Hansard he will find that I took the very same position on the occasion to which he alludes that I have taken to-night.

My remarks-and I applied them correctly-had reference to the attitude taken by certain hon. gentlemen opposite. I said that they were taking a somewhat different position from the one they took the other night. Possibly I may not have done justice to my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) in that respect; but my impression of the discussion the other night was that the claim was put forward principally on the ground that there were a number of people-residents of certain constituencies in New Brunswick and elsewhere-who were unable to inform
themselves in regard to the proclamation and instructions issued at election time because they could not read the English language. I repeat again that so far as my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's is concerned he is perfectly willing for all other people to remain in that condition of ignorance excepting those of French origin. In that respect I might point out that in so far as hon. gentlemen opposite agree to the position taken by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, they are not quite so kindly disposed towards the people in this country of alien enemy birth as they were yesterday when another matter was in question. They were very solicitous in regard to certain people in this country when discussing another clause of this Franchise Act; they are not so solicitous in regard to those people when it comes to discussing this particular matter.
Now, I want for a few moments to discuss the question from the other standpoint- and the only other standpoint from which, it seems to me, it should be discussed. Is this a question of constitutional right? My hon. friend from Three Rivers is very emphatic in declaring that in his opinion it is. I think I am stating that correctly.
Yes.

Well, my hon. friend
has a perfect right, to that opinion, and I am sure that he will concede to me the right to differ from him. And, Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to say to my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) that if I choose to hold a different opinion in regard to this matter, I do not think he should accuse me of being narrow-minded and arrogate to himself great breadth of vision. Because in this regard I am in very distinguished company-I cannot help but think that I am in the company of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who in his long parliamentary career evidently did not take the view which hon. gentlemen opposite have taken; because had he done so I think he would have adopted measures to give to his French-Canadian compatriots the rights which these hon. gentlemen claim they have under the constitution.
I want to quote an expression of opinion by Senator Belcourt in regard to this very matter, and it seems to me that his opinion has all the greater weight because evidently it was voiced by him with considerable regret. He said:
The true fact, regrettable as It may be, is that for the federal domain and the provincial domain of Quebec there is but the constitution which defines enuality of both languages at the

Dominion Parliament, at the Quebec Parliament, before the federal tribunal or courts; and also before the courts of the province of Quebec is the French language on an equal footing with the English language.
Section 133 of the British North America Actwhich has been referred to here by several hon. members to-night

-which proclaims equal rights of the French and English before the federal House, the federal courts and before the provincial House of Quebec and the provincial courts, and in section 93 of the same Act, which gives to each province the exclusive power to legislate in matters of education, constitute the sum total of the rights officially recognized in favour of the French-Canadian people of the Dominion of Canada; these are the only rights recognized in favour of our race; they are the only rights which cannot be stripped from us without the intervention of the Imperial Parliament; they are the only rights which the constitution and the law formally guaranteed to us; they are the only rights which the law will permit us to exact and about which it gives us the means whereby to exact the same.
I am giving the words of Senator Bel-court whose position and attitude in regard to the bilingual question no person can question-and a similar interpretation has already been given very clearly by the hon. minister (Mr. Guthrie). As far as I can see, at all events, there is no manner of doubt as regards the constitutional rights of French Canadians to the use of their language in the province of Quebec as laid down by the constitution. No person has thought of depriving them of those rights. In my judgment, hon. members are seeking to read into that constitution words which I cannot see there-and my eyesight to-night is better than the eyesight of my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) was last night.
It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say that the French language stands on a different footing in this country from any other language except English. That I am quite willing to concede. The manner in which, and the degree to which, the French language stands on that different footing is very clearly laid down in the constitution; and I want to be distinctly understood as expressing my opinion that outside of those constitutional provisions the French language, as such, has no more right to be used, we will say, in the province of Saskatchewan, or the province of Alberta, or the province of Ontario, than has any other language. I ask my hon.- friends not to put words in my mouth which I do not use;
I say there is no constitutional right-if this is to be argued from the sentimental standpoint, that is another matter entirely, and everybody has a right to his ODinion.

But I am challenging the position taken by the hon. members from Kent, N.B., Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), and St. James (Mr. Rinfret) who have argued that the French language has a constitutional right equal to that of the English language in any province of the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

I do not want to be mis-' quoted. I never argued that the French language was on a par with the English language in every province. I argued that every document of this House should be printed in French as well as in English, and I claim that electoral documents are documents of record. It turns on the word "record".

Then I say that a proclamation is not a "record" of this House. It may be presumptuous for me to advance my opinion against that of a lawyer, but I have done so before and escaped with my life, and I shall do so again. I do not regard a proclamation as a record of this House; my hon. friend does. Very well, we must agree to differ. I hope that my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) will not charge me with narrow-mindedness because I do not agree with my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). It is quite natural for my hon. friend from St. James to consider that all the breadth of vision is to be found on his side of the House, as it is also quite natural for him to think that only those who agree with the hon. member for St. James are to be included in the class of broad-minded men, while those who differ from him belong to the class called narrow-minded. My hon. friend may entertain that opinion if he chooses. I understand that he is a very able lawyer, but if I, as a layman, might venture to say so, he is not very logical in putting forth his claim along that line.

I understand that my hon. friend has referred to me as a lawyer.
I am proud to say that I am a newspaper man.
I am very glad indeed to hear my hon. friend say that he is not a lawyer.
So are we.
What have they done to you?

I think my hon. friend would be quite justified in rising to a question of privilege when I said he was a lawyer. However, I was under the impression that he was a lawyer. There are

many in the House who would think that my hon. friend ought to take that as a very great compliment.
If we are to consider this matter from the standpoint of convenience, there are in the western provinces thousands of people of different nationalities who have proved themselves to be first-class citizens, who have endeavoured to do their part since coming to this country. Not all have done this, but many have. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) would have the proclamation issued in French in Alberta where, according to the last census, there were some 19,000 French people, but he would not have it printed in Scandinavian, although there are 28,000 Scandinavians in that province. Nor would he permit it to the Austrians and Germans, who number' 26,000 and 36,000 respectively. In Saskatchewan there are 68,000 Germans, 41,000 Austrians, 33,000 Scandinavians and only 33,000 French Canadians, but my hon. friend says most emphatically that he would not consent to the printing of the proclamation in Scandinavian, Austrian or any other than the French language. Mr. Chairman, it does not make fo-r unity in this country to have these proclamations printed in these several languages. I venture to say that the proposing of this amendment will have served the purpose of hon. gentlemen opposite, broad-minded though they be, if it has given them for the next election something in the nature of a grievance to parade before their electors. I venture to say that some of them have that in mind, just as it was a part of a well-laid plan when the present member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) in 1916 moved his bilingual resolution in this House-he was paving the way for something that he could present to the electors of the province of Quebec in order to solidify them and hold them together. So that, if hon. gentlemen are thinking along that line, why, the purpose of their resolution will be served.
Now, I recognize the value of being able to speak more than one language. But I want to tell my hon. friends that one difficulty standing in the way of just such moves as the move they are making here to-day is found in the fact that they couple their language and their religion together in such a way as to deprive certain people from living in certain parts of this country. Let me repeat, that, so that my words will be distinctly understood. There are certain places in the province of Ontario; there are certain places in other portions of this Dominion, where English-speaking people cannot live.
because conditions make it impossible for them to live there.
What does my hon. friend mean?
My hon. friend should be the last one to ask that; he knows perfectly well what I mean.

I do not know.

that in certain sections of the county of Prescott, represented by my hon. friend, it is impossible for an English-speaking Protestant to live and raise his children, because of the fact that there is only one school for those children to go to, and that is a school in which the French language predominates and in which the Roman Catholic catechism is taught. I am not criticizing or saying anything in regard to any man's religion,-

I am stating candidly and honestly what I believe to be a serious objection to just such movements as this movement which is being made here to-day. I was answering my hon. friend (Mr. Proulx) by saying that in certain sections of the country where you have a separate school system and certain church dogma taught, and where you have a certain language as the language of communication and instruction, you make it impossible for Englishspeaking persons to live in that section of the country. We have had numerous examples throughout Canada; because of the conditions I have indicated persons have been obliged to leave sections of the country and seek home6 elsewhere. That is what I

say; my hon. friend understands perfectly the point that I am making. I am not making it in any spirit of harshness at all; I am using it as I believe I am entitled to use it. -
But the English language is taught in all those schools.

There is no use in
discussing this point further, Mr. Chairman. I was using it merely as an argument. I thought I had made myself perfectly clear in regard to it. There does seem to me to be a very great difference, I may tell my hon. friend, in that matter. A person may go into an English section and there is nothing to interfere; the children will hear nothing from morning till night which will cause offence. I think I have made my point clear. But I will say this in regard to this matter of the French language and its use and its recognition: if my hon. friends opposite who are concerned in regard to the use of this language will use their influence to dissociate their language from the prevailing religion of their province so that we can have non-sectarian schools, then they will very largely remove any opposition there would be to the extension and the general use of the French language throughout this country. I leave that with my hon. friends in order that they may consider and weigh it well.
I want to point out to the Government that there is no use in shutting our eyes to certain definite and well-known facts. There is a feeling in Ontario-whether that feeling is rightly or wrongly founded-against bilingualism. There is a feeling in the western provinces somewhat along the same line. In Manitoba it has manifested itself. There they have a one-language school; that represents public opinion in Manitoba. In Saskatchewan and Alberta they have been and are making strenuous efforts to bring the foreign population there to the point of recognizing the public school and the English language.
As a matter of constitutional right, my hon. friend's contention is not well founded, that the French language should have a recognition ahead of all other languages in other parts of the country than the provinces named in the constitution. I cannot conceive of such a thing as this House of Commons, this Parliament, deliberately agreeing to placard the Dominion of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific with proclamations in half a dozen or a dozen different languages at every election. That would be giving a certain amount of encouragement to 
certain people who are coming to this country to make their homes here, and I do not think that would be in the interest' of Canada, nor would it help in unifying the people of this country. Therefore, I am opposed to the amendment. The people of New Brunswick may be put to a certain inconvenience, tout I cannot think, according to all I have heard with regard to that province, there is much difference in the population now from what it was at the last election or in the election of 1911. Somehow or another they got along with the proclamation as it was at those times and we heard nothing in the way of complaint. If those hon. gentlemen are so much concerned about people of different nationalities being unable to _ read the proclamation in English, it 'will not cost them very much to put their hands into their own pockets and they themselves defray the cost of having the proclamation printed in half a dozen different languages. But it is another matter when you recognize this as a constitutional right, and I am not prepared to accept the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite, namely, that they are merely asking for what is their right under the constitution. Let them
10 p.m. convince me of that and I will fall in line at once without any further word. I am not convinced of that, and I maintain, although I am not a lawyer, that my argument in this regard is sound, that you cannot give to different races in this country certain privileges which they ask, without, to a certain extent, depriving others of constitutional rights which they enjoy under the British North America Act. My rights and theirs are, to a certain extent, relative, one to the other, and if, on sentimental or any other grounds, you give to any group, certain privileges to which they are not entitled under the constitution, by doing so you are depriving me of some of the rights which I hold under the constitution.

(Translation) :	Mr. Chairman, I hope you will
overlook the many errors I am liable to make when I rise to address this House in a language which is not my mother tongue. I intend adding my feeble voice in support of the request made by the revered member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon).
Mr. Chairman, in addressing the House in a tongue which is not my own, I am in the first place encouraged by the example given by the Acting or Outgoing-d do not know which-Prime Minister, who has of late, on many occasions, expressed his

mind in the language of Moliere. I am further encouraged to do so toy the example given by my French-speaking colleagues on this Side of the House, who use the language of Shakespeare with a fluency which all the members of the House of Commons of Canada envy them.
I do not to-night propose to present a very technical argument upon the constitutionality of the question now before the House. I intend to appeal to my fellow-members' spirit of justice and generosity. We live in a bilingual country. In federal matters both languages are on the same footing. As Sir John A. Macdonald once said, "In Canada we have no dominant race," and, in consequence, we have no dominant language. If we consider such a condition as admitted, what is the inference? We have two official languages. The proclamation is an official document which is published in order that every subject, every citizen, may understand it. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) says: "If you take that ground, then you will have to print this document in German and all the languages of the different nationalities, of the different races who live in Canada." Not at all, Mr. Chairman, not at all. The French people hold in this country a position very different from that of the Germans, the Austrians, the Italians and others. I appeal to the history of my country; I appeal to the leading men of the I7th century who are called Champlain, Maisonmeuve, La Salle. After all, the inhabitants of the province of Quebec weTe the foremost pioneers of the land; they have in this country a right which the other new-comers do not possess. That was admitted when the country was transferred over to England; it was admitted at Confederation, and the two races, the French Canadian race and the English or Scotch or Irish-Canadian race are on the same footing, both languages are on the same footing in federal matters.
It is a pleasure for me to point out Quebec as an example. I dare mention the name of Quebec! A few years ago the name of Quebec was spurned throughout the whole Dominion, but to-day it is said to. be the last fortress of liberty and civilization. In the province of Quebec we have municipalities where you can find Frenchmen, or Tather Canadians, who speak French and Canadians who speak English. In these municipalities all notices are printed in both languages'; but where the population is entirely of either language, in such municipalities the 'Lieutenant-Governor, in Council may enact that only one language
can be used. That is common sense; this practice is consistent with good sense. We ask for the enforcement of that practice in the present case.
We have in this country of ours some people who are beset, if I am allowed to use that expression, with the fear that the English language may suffer. Mr. Chairman, I am a Canadian of Scotch descent; the English language is my mother-tongue, and notwithstanding the fact that the French language is as beautiful and clear as spring water, the tongue of Moliere is not superior in my estimation to the tongue of Shakespeare or Milton. Even if there should be a certain amount of rivalry between the two forms of speech, my mother-tongue has nothing to fear.

May I
ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly, with pleasure.
Does the hon. member agree with my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), as to the interpretation to be given to the word "only" in the section under discussion?

I think I have somewhat wasted my oratorical effort on the hon. member from Perth (Mr. Morphy) for I said at the beginning of my remarks that I did not intend to bring forward technical arguments in this discussion. I believe that the hon. member for Three Rivers is right as usual, yet I want to say this: I am not here to follow the example of the Scribes and Pharisees of old, who scrutinized only the letter of the law; I want to appeal to-day to the spirit of the law, to the sense of justice and to the sense of fairness of my fellow-citizens.
The opponents of the French language in Canada to-day, bring forward especially two arguments in every discussion that arises. The first argument is founded on apprehension. Some people are afraid that the English language may lose some ground in this country through the spread of the French language in this country. If I be permitted, let me call the attention of this House to the fact that the people in the province of Quebec are endeavouring to learn the English language. A lot of my French-speaking friends, in. the city of Montreal, see to it that their children are taught in English, even at the same time or even before they are taught their mother tongue. In the province of Quebec, we are anxious to speak English. Such apprehen-

sions as were mentioned a moment ago are absolutely groundless. The other argument brought forward by the opponents of the French language is founded upon hope. Those people entertain the view that a wider and stouter national spirit will be fostered with only one rather than two languages in this country. Permit me, Mr. Chairman, to give the House two illustrations in this regard. You have only one language in Ireland; I believe that is the Connaught and Ulster provinces, only the English language is spoken. But notwithstanding the fact the population of the whole of Ireland speaks one language only, have they succeeded in creating a feeling of harmony between the various nationalities living in that country? Unfortunately, no. I shall give you another illustration: Take Switzerland, that magnificent little republic of Switzerland. Three official languages thrive in that country: German, French and Italian, and I think that republic of Switzerland is fired by a national spirit as vigorous as that existing in any country in the world.
I am very grateful to you, Mr. Chairman, for the kindly attention you have given to my remarks. I beg those of my hon. friends who noticed my too numerous mistakes to excuse me, and I thank the others who did not understand my remarks for the patience they have shown.
Would the hon. member be good enough to repeat that speech in English? I am sure it must be very good.
I would be very glad to repeat it, except that it would be an imposition on those members who have so kindly listened to me in French.
Mr. Chairman, is it not against the rules to repeat the same thing in the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a rule oi the House which declares that an hon. member must not repeat his own arguments or the arguments of any other member. The hon. member for Brome very politely declined to repeat his speech in English, and therefore followed very closely the rule of the House.
The question of the hon. member for Carleton was out of order.

This question which has aroused so much antipathy between the French and English in this country ought surely some day to be treated seriously. As hinted by the hon. member for Fron-
[Mr. McMaster.f
tenac (Mr. Edwards) it has been used largely in the past as election ammunition. It is too serious a matter for that. The English regard the French with too much affection and respect to treat it otherwise than seriously.
Do you think so?

And I hope the French will treat the English a little more seriously. So far the only hon. member who has endeavoured to put this question upon firm ground is the hon. member for Three Rivers. He argues the question as a matter of constitutional right, a right which the French Canadian has had created for him. He has had no other rights created for him than laid down in the law. The hon. member for St. James, and, I am sorry to say, my old friend the hon. member for Gloucester, the hon. member for Kent, N.B., and others, have persisted in dragging in sentiment-they are asking to have this right extended as one of privilege or favour. But the hon. member for Three Rivers repudiates it as a favour, and stands upon his legal right, and with that course I agree. Far be it from me or any other man who has any respect for justice to wish to see the French Canadians or anybody else rifled of their rights under the constitution. When they think those rights are being taken from them, let them appeal to the proper tribunal and have an interpretation given, and the rights restored, if necessary. But this perennial course of insinuation, this everlasting innuendo, this effort to widen the cleavage between the two races, is absolutely wrong and absolutely unjust. We want to give the French their rights. I cannot repeat too often, we insist upon giving the French their rights.
We can look after that all right.
The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) was able to take care of himself during the war.
Possibly, but my hon. friend prides himself on being an Irishman, not a Frenchman. I am talking to the French Canadians.	*
All oppressed people sympathize with each other.

If hon. gentlemen are going to interrupt in this way, let them carry on the debate. I wish to say further that when we have reached this firm ground of constitutional right, we must continue to

respect it. It is set out in detail, and if it is not clear, it is capable of being made clear by, the proper tribunal. To introduce therefore, an amendment at the present time which directly purposes to extend rights, really means that the rights do not exist, and, therefore, on behalf of the French Canadians I repudiate the amendment. If you try to extend rights and admit that you are trying to extend them, as this hon. member who has interrupted so frequently has said-he said that the law was being made here to-night-
Undoubtedly.

-I say it is not being made here to-night. That is how this whole question is being bedevilled by people insisting on jumping up and interjecting new laws into the constitution every little while with respect to things which can only be-

I wish to correct the statement of my hon. friend. I did not say that we were initiating a right; I only said that we were at present working on an electoral act, that that is the law we are now making. I did not express any opinion as to whether we had this right previously or not. I only said we were making an electoral act.

Then I do not understand, as you will readily see, Mr. Chairman, the purport of his previous interruption, or interjection, or intervention, or whatever you choose to call it. I say further, it is high time that the French^Can-adians rested upon the letter of the law and stood upon their rights. If they think they are not obtaining those rights, let them ask for an interpretation and insist on getting them, and we will back them up. But they are placing us in a position where they charge us with being narrowminded and prejudiced, when as a matter of fact we are here charged with the responsibility of maintaining the law as it stands. That law is well defined. It has been admirably set out by the hon. member for Three Rivers. It is this idea of bringing in all sorts of little sentimental appeals to our sympathy and indulgence, to our generosity, broad-mindedness and liberal-spiritedness, that makes the question not one of law, not one of right, but one of sympathy. It then becomes a political football, to be used at election time, or any other time, throughout this country. Just so sure as those gentlemen insist on making this a matter of sympathy, a matter of natural right, and not of legal right, just so sure as they succeed in establishing that, I, for my part, will vote the Norwegian, and the Scandinavian, and the Italian, and everybody else the same natural rights, because natural rights are not legal rights, but rights that belong by the very nature of the case. These other people have the same natural rights as the Frencli-Canadian or the English-Canadian, but they have not the legal rights that the French-Canadians or the Engl'ish-Canadians have. Let the FrenchnCanadians therefore insist upon their legal right. Let them stick to that, and not endeavour, as in this case, to introduce amendments that may go very far in the direction of impairing the very rights which they at present enjoy.

In dealing with this
clause, I think the members of the committee ought to bear in mind that this is a federal, and not a provincial matter, and secondly, that we are actually engaged in framing a new electoral law for Canada. This House and this committee are therefore perfectly free to insert in this new electoral law whatever clauses they deem fit.
The hpn. member for Frontenac founded the main argument of his speech on the basis of what might have happened in previous years in several provinces of Canada. He spoke of the province of Manitoba and the province of Ontario. I say that this House and this committee are not concerned with what might have happened in the province of Manitoba or the province of Ontario, because we are dealing with the French language as it should be dealt with by the House of Commons of Canada, and there is a wide distinction to be observed.
The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), with great generosity, which we certainly will not forget, speaking, as he said, on behalf of and in the name of the French-Canadians, said that he repudiated the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Gloucester, who wishes to amend the clause now under consideration to protect the rights of some of his constituents. I may say to the hon. member for West Peterborough that we on this side of the House are better qualified and better posted to speak on behalf and in the name of the FrenchjCanadians, not only of Quebec, but of all Canada. We do not repudiate the amendment, we stand by it, by every word that it contains. As far as I am concerned, I would go further than the hon. member for Gloucester. I would ask this House, as the hon. member for Three Rivers has asked, to say, not simply that the proclamation by the re-

turning officer shall be printed in English and French in the provinces, of Quebec and Manitoba and in certain other sections of the country where the French population is large enough, but my contention is that according to the constitution as it reads to-day, and as it has been since Confederation, from the Pacific to the Atlantic ocean the French and English languages are on an equal footing in federal matters. Let us have a clause in accordance with the provisions of the existing law, not mentioning the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba at all, or the languages in which the proclamation is to be printed, but simply say that the Chief Electoral Officer shall issue a proclamation in the various constituencies of Canada. I am not aware of any law which exists to-day which says that the proclamations ought to be printed in both languages in the nine provinces of Canada.
Before I discuss this proposition on its merits I wish to preface my argument with another remark. The Acting Solicitor General and other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House talked about privileges and favours. We stand in this House not asking for favours or privileges'; we are only seeking the legal recognition of our actual rights. 'The French minority in Canada is a minority that has an historical past. Our forefathers have written in the history of Canada pages that are beautiful enough to justify their children when they rise in the House of Commons not to seek favours but simply to urge their rights, and that is what we are doing. When I heard hon. members on the other side of the House saying that if the French language is to be used in proclamations in other provinces than Quebec and Manitoba, the proclamations would also have to be/ printed in Italian, German or Austrian, I felt that those who presented such an argument offered an insult to French Canadians and had forgotten the achievements of the French-Canadian people ever since Canada was discovered. We do not stand on the same level as the foreigner who has emigrated within the last fifty or one hundred years. Our forefathers came here when Canada was nothing but a wilderness, and if to-day Canada is a great and prosperous country the English as well as the French people of Canada owe it to those French pioneers who were the first to have the courage to explore its forests and change the wilderness that then existed into the beautiful cities and country districts that we now see. We have had

enough of this argument. I do not know whether it is due to the ignorance of hon. members on the other side, I do not say that it is due to their bad faith; but 1 do say that any man who dares in the House of Commons or anywhere else to pretend that the French Canadians are an inferior race, no matter what position he occupies, is entirely ignorant of the history of this country. We are here, at home. We have been at home in Canada for the last four centuries, and we will remain here, at home, no matter what people in other provinces want or wish. The province of Quebec is to-day setting an example to the rest of the country. For three years insults were hurled in the face of the Freneh-Cana-dian people. To-day we hear from every side, from every direction, from every lip, compliments to the French Canadian race. Compliments or insults will not disturb our equanimity of mind. We have our rights, and we will stand by them, and insist on them.
I said, Mt. Chairman, that constitutionally speaking the French language in Canada had rights, and rights superior to those of any other nation, and I will prove it. Look up the treaty, wffiieh was signed on the battlefield of Montreal, -when that city was handed to the British troops; look up the treaty which was further signed at Paris; look up the Act of Quebec which was guaranteed by the British authorities in 1775; look up these documents and in each of them it will be found that the French population of Canada are guaranteed the enjoyment of their language.
That is not right.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon?
. Mr. EDWARDS: I say that is not right.
If the hon. gentleman is not of my opinion I would be very grateful if, instead of saying I am not right, he would support his statement with facts; I am perfectly willing to hear him.

I am prepared to do so. ,1 merely dissent from the hon. gentleman's very explicit and emphatic statement. He makes a most emphatic statement, which I most emphatically deny, I say that in the Quebec Act of 1774, and in the other Acts to which he refers, there is no mention of language. I have read those Acts as well as my hon. friend.

When the hon. member read those Acts he may have read them in

the same way- as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) read the Ontario Act which was referred to in the discussion last night. I have read those documents, Mr. Chairman, and I say that from e very moment that the British troops were in this country victorious conventions or agreements were signed in the city of Montreal toy the general commanding the British army and the general commanding the French army by which the rights of the French population were guaranteed front that very moment.
The hon. gentleman does not say that "language" iwas mentioned.
I say that at that time there was ta mention of our laws, our religious customs and our language.
No, sir.
Yes.

At Paris the same thing was done. In 1774 when the Quebec Act was passed-any hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) will not deny it-the customs existing in Lower Canada at that time as to laws, as to religion, and as to language, were secured by that Act. Let us go further, Mr. Chairman, in the history of our country; let us go to 1791 when the first Legislative Assembly iwas convened in Lower Canada. At that time-just as upon the present occasion in this Parliament- though nearly 150 years have elapsed-in the Legislative Assembly of Quebec in 1791 there were members like the hon. members for Frontenac, North Perth, and West Peterborough here, who thought that the rights of the French language should not exist-. A gentleman by the name Eich-ardson got up and made a speech in which my hon. friend from Frontenac may have found all his arguments, the arguments he gave us to-night. This gentleman, Mr. Chairman, in 1791, wanted to treat the French people as an inferior race in their own country. But the question was settled in [DOT] that year. I would ask the hon. members of this House to read the speeches delivered at that time when it was decided that the French language and the English language should be used in the Legislative Assembly as guaranteed by the existing laws.
The year 1840 gave us our next constitutional enactment. Lord Durham had come to Canada, and he thought that a good method of unifying Canada was to force the two races in this country to speak but one language. The recommendations of his report are'well known; I will not take up the time of the House in enumerating them. Under the Union Act as passed the French language was excluded from the House of Parliament. What happened? The French people protested, and When Lafontaine, that great patriot from Quebec, became the Premier of Canada, and when the province of Ontario gave a real Liberal whose name ,was Baldwin-when Baldwin and Lafontaine formed the great ministry of the Union party, for in those days men came from Ontario who were not afraid of standing for equal rights and equal privileges for ,botih races in this country, and when Baldwin supported Lafontaine, the Union Act was changed and the French language was restored t-o its former position in Canada. Ever since that day, Mr. Chairman, the beautiful and magnificent language of Racine, Corneille, and Moliere has been heard, and heard legally, in our Houses of Parliament.
We now -come to Confederation. We have had the British North America Act quoted in this House to-night by hon. gentlemen on both sides. The British North America Act, as you, Mr. Chairman, know, is the reproduction of the resolutions passed by the conference at Quebec in 1864, resolutions agreed to by the representatives of the provinces of Canada then convened in the city of Quebec-that is the provinces oi Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario-resolutions which were reconsidered at another conference held at Westminster Hotel in London; and finally these resolutions, after having been considered-by the Canadian Parliament, were enacted and embodied in what is called to-day -the British North America Act. There was one man in Canada who worked-and worked his very hardest

for the achievement of this great thing which we call Confederation, and that man was Sir John A. Macdonald, who had as his right hand man, as everybody knows, Sir George Etienne Cartier. In the House of Parliament -at that time this question of language was raised. If hon. gentlemen will refer to the Confederation debates they will see that Hon. Mr. Evanturel rose in the House and asked what about the rights of the French language. "According to these resolutions, -and according to the Act which will be passed by the Imperial Parliament, will the rights of the French language be secured and guaranteed?" These are the words spoken in reply by Sir John A. Macdonald, Father of Confederation, and the promoter of -the British North America Act.:

Hon. Attorney General Macdonald: I desire to say that I agree with my hon. friend that as it stands just now the majority governs; but in order to cure this, it wras agreed at the conference to embody the provision in the Imperial Act. (Hear, hear.) This was proposed by the Canadian Government, for fear an accident might arise subsequently, and it was assented to by the deputation from each province that the use of the French language should form one of the principles upon which the Confederation should be established, and that its use, as at present, should be guaranteed by the Imperial Act. (Hear, hear.)
We have here, Mr. Chairman, an express declaration from the then Premier of our country to the effect that the Imperial Act, and the resolutions on which the Imperial Act is based, recognized as a fundamental principle of Confederation the privileges of the French language as they existed at the time of Confederation. For, at the time of Confederation, as no hon. member will deny, the French and English languages were the official languages in both Lower and Upper Canada.
The Bill now before us provides that the Chief Electoral Officer will receive the documents and papers from the returning officer presiding at an election in each constituency. These papers are to be kept of record and will remain in the hands of the Chief Electoral Officer for two years. The argument advanced by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is that according to the British North America Act every parliamentary record has to be in French and in English; that this proclamation being a parliamentary record, should therefore be in English and French; and the clause as he said, should read simply that the proclamation will be issued, without mentioning in which language; then, according to the law it would mean that the proclamation would be printed both in English and in French.
I do not wish to detain the House much longer, but Mr. Chairman, I have heard arguments to-night which really astonished me. For instance, if I am not wrong, I heard an hon. gentleman say that if in other provinces the proclamations were issued in more than one language racial disunion would be promoted. During the recent war if any country gave to the rest of the world an example of national honour and of patriotic heroism that country was Belgium. In Belgium there are two official languages. When Belgium fought the invading Germans did the fact that she had two official languages prevent her soldiers from giving an example to the rest of the world which will never be forgotten? I think if Canada can do as well as Belgium in so far as nat-

ional unity is concerned we can rest well satisfied.
As I said before, we are asking, not for privileges or for favours, but for rights. But, even though we were asking for favours or privileges, I think hon. gentlemen on the other side ought to be more generous than the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) seems to be. The French language is not a barbarian tongue. The fact that proclamations were printed in French in British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, New Brunswick and the other provinces would not have a tendency to adversely affect the education of our population. Every man in Canada, if he wishes to be completely educated, ought, like the English people who are highly and completely educated to know both languages. In England no gentleman claims to be completely educated unless he speaks French. And every hon. member knows that most of the difficulties at the Peace Conferene arose from the fact that Mr. Wilson did not understand French.
The time has gone by when we should continue to fight over this language question. We have two races speaking two different languages. Let us admit the fact and let us legislate so as to meet the needs of these two races. Let us have laws that will promote the welfare of our people, and let us forget the past fights over these language and racial questions. The language which was good enough to serve Marshal Foch in the war to give the final orders which meant the victory of the Allies is good enough for any part of this country. I say that a language which is used on every official escutcheon of Canada or of England to show the national motto, Dieu et mon Droit, is good enough for every Canadian. Would the hon. member for Frontenac pretend that we ought to translate Dieu et mon Droit into English, or Honi soit qui mal y pense?
I think that the amendment as presented by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) is fair and ought to carry, for it would be a good piece .of legislation-legislation of a character to appease the agitation that now exists in certain sections of this Dominion.
Mr. EDW'ARDS: Mr. Chairman, I crave the indulgence of the House to make one statement as a matter of record since the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Cannon) and I very distinctly differ on one point. I make this statement, and I am prepared to submit to the humiliation of being shown I am wrong-if I am wrong,

-that in the terms of capitulation after the Battle of the Plains of Abraham; in the terms of capitulation one year later after the fall of Montreal; in the Peace of Paris of 1763; in the Quebec Act of 1774; in the Constitutional Act of 1791 there is not one single word in regard to language or language rights. Ample and generous provisions were made in some of those documents for safeguarding the interests of the Roman Catholic religion, but I repeat that not one word is to be found in any of those documents relative to language rights. I wish to add this further statement, that in the Act of Union of 1840, not only was there no mention of the French language or of the rights of that language, but that Act made distinct and specific provision that the records of the House should be printed in the English language, and the English language only; and that custom prevailed till several years after the Act of Union was passed.

May I ask the hon. member from Frontenac:	Does he think my
offer is a fair one? Since we cannot agree on the interpretation of that section, let, us strike out the words in section 37 as I have suggested, and if the proclamation is published in English only, then we have a grievance, which we will bring before the courts, and the courts will give us an interpretation of the British North America Act.

It is not necessary to
adopt the hon. member's suggestion. I maintain that the clause as it is now and as it has existed for the last thirty or forty years is satisfactory to me, and I see no reason to change it. I do not believe it is in the. best interests of the country to change it. If the hon. gentleman has a constitutional grievance, he has a constitutional remedy for the redress of that grievance.

Mr. Chairman, I have no doubt that the clause as drafted is satisfactory to the hon. gentleman from Frontenac. As was so eloquently put by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) there are two classes of people and two schools of thought in this House and in Canada-one broad-minded and the other narrow-minded. The minister said that some influence had been brought to bear upon him, and of such a nature that he was not able to bring about this amendment which would allow the Chief Electoral Officer to publish the proclamations in both languages. He did not say what this influence was. The hon. member for St. James-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to remarks of mine when he says that some influence was brought to bear upon me?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada

I accept the declaration ol
the hon. gentleman so far as members of this House are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is all I object to.

But I contend that so far
as the rest of my statement is concerned the declaration of the minister is no correction or contradiction of my statement. I take his very words and I say you can draw from them no other inference than that somebody is prejudiced against the use of the French language in this country. But, Sir, this is no surprise to us.
This is not the first time that we have heard in this House and outside of it of gentlemen endeavouring to restrict the use of the French language as it has hitherto been in use. We have had, in many instances, outspoken declarations from hon. gentlemen opposite as well as from people in various parts of this country, endeavouring to liken the French-Canadian group to some kind of Indian, the Six Nations, or the Hurons, or the Crees of the western provinces.
That is not correct.
The hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) says that is not correct.

No, the hon. member
for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). The hon. gentleman is a little narrow tonight.

_ In many sections of this country there are schools of thought which hold that the use of the French language should not only not be extended, but should be restricted, and that the rights which have been enjoyed by the French-Canadian population should be taken away from them, or at least that those rights should be confined to the province of Quebec, just as reserves are set aside for the Indian tribes of this country. Some hon. gentlemen contend that what I say is not true; that no members of this House are opposed to the exercise of those rights; that no section of this country has a tendency to restrict the rights which have * been enjoyed by the French-Canadian population hitherto. We have seen some of those hon.
gentlemen, the very hon. gentlemen who tried to restrict such use, declare themselves to be the defenders of the French-Canadian students who could not get a sufficient education. May I be permitted to cite, for instance, a declaration by the hon. member for Toronto West (Mr. Hoc-ken), as cited in the Citizen of the 6th March? The hon. gentleman said:
We are fighting the battles of the French-Canadian boy and girl.
The hon. member at that time was fighting the battles of the French-Canadian boy and girl. What did this hon. gentleman say under his signature in a document which has been, to his knowledge or not, widely circulated?-a document which is headed: "(Strictly confidential.) To be referred to or read only within the tiled doors of lodge, chapter or precep-tory. Report of the Joint Legislation Com mittee of the Orange Order." This is signed by two members of the House, amongst others and it deals with the very question now under consideration, the use of the French language in the various provinces. The document reads:
Acting in hearty co-operation, as we always do, our own order, through its M.W. Grand Master, Dr. Ellis, and the Royal Black Knights, through their Grand Master, Bro. A. A. Gray, issued an appeal to both memberships to use every legitimate means to secure the support of the members of' Parliament in every constituency for the Military Service Act and the War-time Elections Act. We must see to it that the safeguards of this Election Act are not thrown away when the war is over.
We are urging the Government to see to it that people who, by reason of peace treaties at the close of the war may be entitled to come here from alien countries, should not be enfranchised at all, until they can read and write in the English language and until they sign a document agreeing to obey our laws, learn the English language, have it efficiently taught in their schools, and to forfeit all their property and civil rights and be liable to deportation on conviction of failure in these matters.
Further on the document says:
We have, at the request of our Prince Edward Island brethren, secured the legal opinion of two eminent lawyers on the question of the right to use French in the schools of that province. We believe the opinion will greatly help out Island brethren in their fight against French aggression.
It has become quite apparent that the school situation in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Alberta must be thoroughly investigated, and our brethren in each of these provinces, assisted by legal advice, organization and investigation, so that effective steps may be taken to put an end to Rome's tactics in using French in schools wherever she can.
No doubt you have all read how at the Saskatchewan School Trustees' Convention the tac-

tics of Rome to secure separate schools, bilingual teaching, and other special favours, was triumphantly defeated by the union of the Orangemen, the Sons of England and other loyalists.
This document is absolutely the exposition of the policies of the Orange Order *as regards the use of the French language. It says further:
We have notified the Government that the 446 French signs on p&st offices outside of Quebec, and the 859 bilingual post office signs, also outside of Quebec, must all be removed, as we believe such signs, with any other language on them,-

In answer to the hon. member for West Peterborough, who said it was * not true that the French Canadians were considered as Indians in some parts of this country, and that the province of Quebec was not looked upon as a reserve for them, let me quote from this document with which the committee is cognizant, these words:

has been read. The line which I intended to cite-
