I shall abide by your ruling, Sir, but I might refer hon. gentlemen to the document to establish the fact that French Canadians were accused of taking the place of white men in Ontario and it was declared they should be sent hack to Quebec. If we take the place of white men, that implies that we are not white men, and if we are not white men, we are Indians. That is the argument that I wanted to make on this point-that some gentlemen not only wish to restrict the use of the French language, but to assimilate us to the Indians in this country.
No.
Does not this document say that we have taken the place of white men in Ontario and that we should be sent back to Quebec?

I rise to a point of
order. The hon. member's remarks are not relevant to the clause under discussion.
That is a fine speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order just raised is that the remarks of the hon. member are not relevant to the clause under discussion. I have already drawn the attention of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) to that point. I understand that he has accepted the ruling and is coming back to the subject under discussion.

I made the statement that the French Canadians were in some sections of this country assimilated to Indians, and I referred to the document which you, Sir, prevented me from reading. If I cannot read it I can at all events refer hon. gentlemen opposite to that document in which they will find that the French Canadians

are accused of taking the place of white men in Ontario, and it says that we should be sent back to our Indian reserve, that is to say, the province of Quebec.
Is it not true also that in certain sections of the country some English Canadians were referred to as worse than Huns? I do not think either one was taken very seriously, but is it not a fact?
If I entered upon the ground on which the hon. member is trying to draw me, I would be called to order by the Chair for irrelevancy.
I think you would.
If the hon. member admits that, surely his question must have been irrelevant and out of order?
Out of order, but not irrelevant.

We. are just emerging from a great war, and we are facing almost absolutely new conditions. We are trying in many parts of this country to develop this great Canada of ours to the best of our ability. Who will say that the population of the province of Quebec under 150 years of British rule has not done its share in the development of the natural resources of this country? We had an immense section of this country left to us. We tried to develop it. We tried to imbue our children with respect for law and order, and I think we have been successful in obtaining results. I think there is no section of this country which has done more for the development of Canada than the province of Quebec. It is now for us to decide whether we intend to live in harmony and in co-partnership, on an equal footing with our brothers and co-citizens of the other provinces. The people of the other provinces do not fully understand the mentality and the mind of the French Canadians. If we are willing to work for the development of this country in harmony with our co-citizens of other provinces, at the same time we absolutely refuse to be absorbed or to receive the stamp of any other character than we now possess. We consider that we are true Canadians. If we are true Canadians we should be Canadians not only in the province of Quebec but outside of the province of Quebec. We should not be received in other provinces as foreigners or as chasers of white men. We should be received as partners, and coworkers in the development of this country no matter where we come from, and the rights and privileges which were granted by Confederation should not be restricted, but the constitution should be carried on in spirit and in letter. How can hon. gentlemen from other provinces expect that we shall harmoniously work in sympathy with them when every time any one of our fellow-citizens of French origin goes beyond the limits of the province of Quebec he is treated as an alien, an undesirable, the enemy of the white man and as one who should be sent back to the reserve in the province of Quebec? Every time a group of Canadians of French origin go beyond the limits and boundaries of the province of Quebec and wish to develop the teaching of their maternal tongue, not at the expense of other people but at their own expense, they are restricted by that very narrow-minded class of people to which my hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General was referring when he said that some people in this country were prejudiced against the French language.
We must not be considered an inferior race, because we are not an inferior race. We must not be considered as being here by favouritism, because we are here by right. If others want our co-operation they must cater to our sympathy, they must treat us as we treat others,-they must apply to us the same methods that we use towards the English-speaking minority of the province of Quebec. We are ready to co-operate to make of this Canada of ours a great and prosperous country, but it seems to me that it is not the true patriotic spirit which inspires hon. gentlemen when they attempt to prevent 150,000 French-Canadians in the Maritime Provinces from having the proclamations under this Act published in their own maternal tongue. What would be the objection, what harm could be done, by publishing them in French and English? None. Only this system of restriction, this spirit of antagonism to the French language could inspire the refusal from the treasury benches to accept the amendment, Those who inspire such restrictions are not the best of Canadians.

I have heard the hon. gentleman state several times that some one has referred to the French Canadians as being Indians who should be sent back to the reserve, but I did catch the authority that the hon. gentleman had for making that statement. Who said it? When? And where?

The chairman of this committee prevented me from reading the document. I will refer the hon. gentleman for my authority to a document already on

record in this House and which was put on Hansard at the very opening of this session.

What were the words,
please?

The words were that French Canadians who went to Ontario to take the places of the white men should be sent back to the province of Quebec. I said that these words, that French Canadians had taken the places of white men, impliedly meant that the French Canadians who went to Ontario were not white men and that consequently, if they were not white men, they were Indians.
That is your inference.
I admit, that was an inference.
They might have been of some other colour than that of Indians.

The hon. gentleman may
draw his inference for himself, but I think that common sense and the meaning of plain English will show that a native of this country who is not a white man is a red man and is an Indian by birth. I do not think there is any other imputation that could be made or any other inference that could be drawn from this statement. I consequently say, Sir, that to my mind the minister should accept one or other of the remedies which were proposed to him. I fail to see how any serious objection can be raised to the use of the French language in the proclamations that are going to be issued under this Act except those which might be urged by that narrow-minded view which inspires some sections of this country and the adoption of which sufely will not be beneficial to Canada. Therefore I think the minister should accept one or other of these amendments.

I hope to be able to make a few remarks without you, Mr. Chairman, being under the necessity of calling me to order. I had no intention of speaking to the question, and I would not have done so but for the reference of the last speaker (Mr. Vien) to myself and his remarkable straining and effort to read into the reasonable opposition to the unlimited extension of the French language over Canada a hatred of the French race. I want to say to my hon. friend that there has never been any effort made in this House, from Confederation until the present day, by any person, to restrict the use of the French language to any narrower bounds than those which were set forth, by the Constitution of
TMr. V'en ]
this country. I submit that if my hon. friend and those who sit with him have any desire to promote harmony they will be willing to observe the Constitution in that regard. If they had any larger rights than those which they possess there would be no objection from any province in Canada to going to the full limit that was permitted to them under the Constitution. There is no hatred of the French language, and there is no hatred of the French race. On the contrary, we of the province of Ontario have the very kindliest feelings for the French, but we say that their leaders, one of whom we have listened to to-night, are in the habit of doing-what the hon. gentleman has been doing for the last half hour-their very best to provoke discord between the two races. He has strained and stretched every argument that he could imagine or think of, even charging us with calling the French people Indians, something I never heard of in my life, something I have absolutely no sympathy with and something that I would have resented if I had heard it; but he would put such a phrase as that into the mouths of the people of Ontario. Why? Surely not for the purpose of promoting harmony in this country. If that is his idea of harmony I must say that his education has been seriously neglected on that point.
Will the hon. gentleman tel! me what meaning he put upon that phrase which he signed to the effect that French Canadians who took the places of white men in Ontario should be sent back to Quebec?

I dealt with that when
it was introduced into this House and I do not propose to deal with it again. But I want to repeat my statement that I have no sympathy with any such suggestions as he made in this House, that French Canadians should be regarded-
Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question?

No. He seems to object that we should have any regard for the young boys and girls of French Canada. If we have anything that we think is better than they have why should we not give it to them? Why should we not desire above everything else that in Quebec and in every other province of Canada a high type of civilization should prevail and if we have something that is better than what they have why should we not offer it to them?
We have contended at times, Mr, Chairman, that the educational system of Quebec is not such as the French boys and

girls should have, that it did not fit them, or rather fit the masses of the people for the higher employments of life. Now if we .were antagonistic, and had any feeling of hatred to the French race we would not take any action at all; we would let the French race be the hewers of wood and the drawers of water. But we take the ground that this can never be a great and powerful country unless education is widely diffused, and that every boy and girl-no matter where they are or what language they apeak-shall have a complete education that will fit them to take high places in this country. If my hon. friend objects to that, then I submit he is objecting to the very kindliest instincts that to-day are entertained with regard to his race. It is not, as my hon. friend suggests, that we object to French Canadians coming into the province of Ontario; but it is that we object to them corning in and bringing certain peculiar customs that, among the provinces of Canada, prevail only in the province of Quebec, and seeking to establish in those other provinces institutions that are foreign to the temper of the people, and-I want to say to him-institutions that they will resist as long as they have any power to do ,so. The province of Quebec is large enough, Mr. Chairman, to comfortably contain three or four times the population that it accommodates to-day. If my hon. Ifriend desires for his people that they shall carry their customs with them wherever they go, then I say the only way to do that is for them to fill up the unsettled areas of their own province. 'Then they can live under their parish system, then they can enjoy all these peculiar laws which seem to please them, and there will be no word of protest uttered from any quarter whatever. No man has ever proposed that the people of the other provinces should go down into Quebec and alter the laws of that province -the educational law' or any other. There has never been any attack made upon the province of Quebec since Confederation; it has always been in the other direction; there has been one constant agitation in this country for fifty years to get additional privileges for the French language, and for the establishment of these customs to which we object.
Now my hon, friend wants these proclamations printed all over Canada in French as well as in English. Let me point out a most serious objection to that which I have not yet heard mentioned. In every western province there is to-day the very
strongest sentiment against bilingualism whether it has reference to Polish, German, Austrian or French. The people of Western Canada want to speak one language from the Great Lakes to the Pacific ocean. They have made great headway in teaching the Polish, the Euthenian, and the children of other nationalities, the English language which is the language of this country, especially of that part of Canada. Now let it be said, Sir, by federal enactment, that there is another language than English which has a special provilege or a special standing in this country, and you strengthen and encourage all the racial agitations that have been carried on in the western provinces foi the last fifteen or twenty years, and you nullify the effects of the splendid work that has been done by the Government of Hon. T. C. Norris in Manitoba, where they have established a system of schools by which every child- whether Austrian, German, or any other nationality learns the English language and upon attaining the age of twelve can go out into the market place and do business in the language of this country. I want to tell the hon. gentleman the moment he introduces another language into Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia he only gives encouragement to that multitude of foreigners of various languages to carry on their agitation. They will say:, "Aha, there is another language that is recognized. All we have to do is to keep fighting and we will get that privilege for ourselves." The most natural thing in the world, Mr. Chairman, for them to say. And, instead of promoting harmony in the West, it would set up a state of discord that would be very difficult to allay or remove. That, in my judgment, is one of the cardinal reasons for objecting to the use of the French or any other language than English in these proclamations. Not only that, but go down into the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. There, in spite of the law, French schools are being operated; the law is openly defied by the operation of bilingual schools. A very large part of the population object to that, but this kind of a proclamation would only give those schools additional standing.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that a clause in the Franchise Act that was good enough for Sir Wilfrid Laurier ought to be good enough for my hon. friends opposite. Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not put the French language on an equality with the English language in the election proclamations. Why did he not do that? There are only

two reasons that I can think of: One was he knew it would be an unconstitutional act, and the other was that he feared, or hesitated, to antagonize that sentiment which would be offended by the spreading of French proclamations all over the province of Ontario. But my hon. friends opposite want that done, knowing full well that this Government could not do any one thing that would so incense the people of the province of Ontario against them as to spread French proclamations all over that province.

Why would they be
incensed?

For this reason:	We
know in the province of Ontario that for fifty years the French leaders have been trying to get exactly what they are trying to get here to-night-further official recognition for their language beyond the limits of the constitution,-and the people of the provinces outside of Quebec will not have that if they can prevent- it. They want the French language to stand where it is under the British North America Act. They will not endeavour to curtail it any more than it is curtailed by that Act, but they say they are not going to permit if they can prevent it, any further extensions in the other provinces. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not prepared to face the probable loss of votes that would certainly have taken place in Ontario if he had spread French proclamations over the country. It was either that, Sir, or because he knew that to do so would be absolutely unconstitutional.
It is quite true, as my hon. friends opposite say, that we have two races in this country, which races they tell us must live together. If that is so, Mr. Chairman, it can only be by each respecting the rights of the other. Neither can deprive the other of any rights that they have under the constitution; and when one race gets special privileges that infringes upon the rights of the other race, then I say they are taking sure and certain steps to create discord in this Dominion. There is a way that my hon. friends can promote harmony in this country: It is by standing upon those guarantees for their language, for their customs, and for the protection of their religion-for everything that, they have in Quebec-standing right where they were put in 1867. I want to tell my hon. friends that Confederation could never have been formed unless the leaders in the province of Quebec had consented to the terms that are embodied

in the Confederation Act to-day. The representatives from the other parts of this country would not have conceded anything more than they did concede,-and he knows that as well as I do. It was not Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir George Cartier who together brought about Confederation : the late George Brown and other men had something to do with it, and they exercised their influence, which influence was all exerted to restrict the use of the French language to where it is to-day; and where it is to-day, Mr. Chairman, is where it ought to stay-it is where it must stay unless my hon. friends opposite intend to cause more serious disruption in this country.
They talk about us people in Ontario being prejudiced against the French language. I resent that statement; we have no prejudice against the French language. But I do not think we need more than the exhibition we have had to-night to prove, Sir, that there is a very distinct prejudice on the other side in favour of the French language. Its supporters are trying to push it in where it has no right to be. They are trying, as did the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), to strain language to prove that this election proclamation is a "record" of the House. A more absurd argument I think I never heard. An election proclamation is a record of an election, but it is not a record of this House, and could not be construed in that way. But it is that everlasting straining of every point that comes up, to force further language concessions, that creates all the difficulty between the two races. I appeal to my hon. friends to accept the Act of Confederation as it stands. Let them be as loyal to it as we are in Ontario, and there will be no trouble between these two provinces.
The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) made a proposition that we should leave out all mention of languages so that he could have a grievance. Why is he looking for a grievance? No one over here has been asking for a grievance-something to be done that would give us a chance to go to the courts. I think that we on this side of the House have shown an entirely different spirit. Besides, if my hon. friend wants to go to the courts, and if, as he argues, an election proclamation is a record of this House, then he can go to the courts and have it so declared; and having it so declared he will get what he wants. The way is open for him to take some particular action to get what he wants

under circumstances that would be more profitable to him and some of his friends in their election contests.
Someone said that a great many women could not read the English language although their husbands could. Well, their husbands can tell them what is in the proclamation. And if those women are living in an English-speaking province they ought to learn to speak English, it ought to be part of their education, if they are ever to be in a position to deal with the people of the province in which they live. I know very well that if I were living in the province of Quebec I would learn to speak the French language. I know that any of my friends who go down to Quebec for any length of time soon learn French, for they must be able to speak and write it in order to do business. Those who come to our province ought to learn our language, and it is no excuse to say that they cannot learn it, and that therefore they must have proclamations of this kind printed in their mother tongue.
I submit that not a single argument has been advanced to-night as to why this clause should not stand exactly as it is. Ii anything, the use of the French language should be prohibited in Manitoba. We have not argued that; we might have done so. I submit that point to prove that we are not looking for a grievance, we are not looking for a quarrel; all the grievances have been sought on the other side, and all the quarrels are being started there. Then isome over-zealous gentleman will stand up and declaim against us for making inroads upon their rights because we are merely refusing to grant them privileges beyond those which their leaders in the most solemn manner fixed in the constitution. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the clause should' carry.

My only regret is, Mr. Chairman, that on this vexed question of language one should have to rely upon treaties or statutory enactments in order to give the minority what it claims is but a natural right. The committee will understand that a minority is always jealous, as might be expected, of the rights it em joys. And when one listens to such arguments as that which we have just been privileged to hear, it is quite natural that the minority would feel somewhat nervous and anxious if it were left to the tender mercies of thehon. gentleman (Mr. Hocken). Why, my hon. friend has just exhibited the spirit which animates him in this discussion by stating very coolly that the section should remain as it is, but that if it were amended he might only amend it in such a way as to eliminate the Manitoba law.
My hon. friend says: But the section has been on the statute books for thirty years and has never been challenged; therefore you should be satisfied with it. Sir, I have yet to learn that there is any statute of Limitations against a natural right-because I am not advocating at the present moment a statutory enactment, nor am I advocating rights which one would enjoy by virtue of a treaty. I know ljy experience what I can expect from certain people when my treaty rights are at stake.
My hon. friend, lording it over us with a superior air, has condescended to lecture the minority. He has compared the respective educational systems of the great province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. I shall not, Mr. Chairman, attempt to answer the arguments of the hon. gentleman, for I know it would be a hopeless task to convince him that at least-at least we are not his inferiors, that at least we should be on a footing of equality.
Quite right.

I shall not for one moment argue that my fellowmen are better than the hon. gentleman's electors; or that the province of Quebec has any educational system superior to that in vogue in the province of Ontario. But would my hon. friend accept the testimony, not of a French Canadian, nor of a Roman Catholic, but the statement of a sturdy Scotch Canadian- and Presbyterian, T suppose? I refer to Sir Andrew MacPhail.
Hear, hear.

Am I right in saying
that he is a good Scotch Canadian?

You could not speak
and give him higher praise.

Not long ago Sir Andrew MacPhail addressed a letter to the London Spectator in answer to such statements as have been made this afternoon-statements made in a letter written by a Mr. Stutfield to the London Spectator. I will quote a few sentences of Sir Andrew MaePhail's letter. Remember, Sir Andrew MacPhail is a Professor of McGill University. He hails from the Maritime Provinces; yes *he is a son of little Prince Edward Island. In answering the slanderous statement made by Mr. Stutfield he said:
The percentage ot school attendance in Quebec is the highest in Canada; crime is the

least prevalent. The allegation that "the "habitant* of Quebec is hopelessly outclassed by Protestant Canadians in trades and professions'' is exactly wrong. Quebec has the most productive farms, the most thrifty and contented workmen, the most successful industries, the most efficient public services in America. Quebec professional men have dominated the Government ever since Confederation by reason of their superior education alone. Within the present month a sum of five million dollars has been raised by voluntary subscriptions for the new French University. By an appeal to the documents all these facts have been verified. The provincial treasurer, himself an English Protestant, will supply them. Of the less specific charges against Quebec I can offer only an opinion, but it is based upon observations extending over a period of thirty years. The people of Quebec-
Will my hon. friend listen to this?
The people of Quebec are most tolerant of all kinds Of education and forms of religion, the least tolerant of fanaticism; they are the best-tempered and the most mannered; the least disposed to interfere with personal liberty; the most stalwart and independent in politics; the most careful in administering justice to rich as well as poor. Quebec is the only place in America which has successfully resisted the emissaries of evil from the labour world of Europe and United States. Quebec is the last refuge in America of good order and political sense. Lastly, the only two churches in Canada which do not "interfere in 'politics'* are the Catholic Church and the Church of Scotland.
I shall not delay the committee by commenting upon this opinion expressed by Sir Andrew MacPhail, but it is a good answer to the rather sneering remarks made by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). My hon. friend claims that he is a promoter of harmony in this country. I wish my hon. friend, in seeking to attain his end, would adopt different means. As one who reads the Orange Sentinel from week to week all the year round, I say, Sir, that my hon. friend is one of the most notorious, one of the most dangerous firebrands that this country has ever known. Yet he is all courtesy; he is all fine manners in the (House; he always speaks with a smile on his face. But the moment he dips his pen into the ink bottle, why, the Roman Catholic church, the French-Canadian papulation, the province of Quebec, all ought to be wiped out from the Dominion of Canada. Is he a promoter of harmony and of good will? My hon. friend ought to reside for a few months, perhaps for a few years, in the good old province of Quebec; there he would learn what is tolerance, what is concord, what is harmony. We have no difficulties with our English-speaking friends. My hon. friend has only one objective with his paper, that is, to promote disunion and discord in Canada; in other words, to make of On-
IM Lemieux.]
tario the Ulster of Canada. Why should we import into Canada the troubles, the ills, the miseries and the woes of the Old World? You shall not make an Ireland of Canada. Now, let us come to the question.
Hear, hear.

I have answered the
arguments of my hon. friend from West Toronto and I think I have been fair with him. The arguments that I have used are not mine; I have quoted from the letter of a fellow-Canadian of a different race and creed from mine.
Now, the amendment which has been proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon; is, I contend, a most reasonable one, and it has been presented in a moderate way. If the committee does not think that it should accept this amendment in its present form, I for one, although I think that it smacks to much of a concession, would be ready to accept, for the sake of harmony, the proviso suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding). And the committee should, I think, respond to the noble appeal made in such a moderate way by my hon. friend. Is it possible that in a British legislature any one should question the common sense interpretation of section 133 of the British North America Act? My hon. friend says that the proclamation fixing the day of the election, fixing the place where the polls are to be located, is not a "record;" it is only part of the record of the election. I contend that the spirit of section 133 is that any federal document must be printed in both languages. The language spoken in this House, the language printed in the statute books, in the Canada Gazette, in the journals and in the records of this House, must be French and English alike. Any member elected to this House may be challenged to appear before a committee of the House if it should appear that gross irregularities or frauds have been committed in that election. I have in mind the Elgin election case, and if I delve into past history, I have in mind the Kamouraska election case, where the returning officer, and other officers who had attended to the elections in those particular cases were summoned before the Committee On Privileges and Elections, and there the documents of the elections were filed, the proclamation was filed-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That surely proves nothing. Any other document may be filed in

this House. Any committee that has power, may call for documents.

It proves that they are part of the records of the House, so much so that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is obliged by law to keep under his control during a certain period of time, I forget how long, perhaps a year, or at least six months,-
One year, two years.
-the election records. They are part of the archives, the records, of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery who has hitherto been required to keep these documents was never an officer of this House.
Is he not a federal officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, a federal officer of the Crown, not of the House of Commons.

Hair-splitting.
Mr. GUTHRIiE: I know this is a legal point, but the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was always, from the days of Cromwell down to the present, an officer apart from the House; he was the Clerk of the Crown as opposed to the Clerk of the Houses of Parliament. I point this out because technically documents in his custody would not be documents of the House.

Who appoints the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery?
Mr. GUTHR'IE: The Governor in Council.
That is, the Dominion Government appoints the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and if he had to be appointed by the Civil Service Commission, he would have to know one of the two languages.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My point is only that, strictly speaking, he is not an officer of this House, if my hon. friend is arguing that point.
My hon. friend will allow me to say that I take this in argu-,ment as a mere quibble. It is unworthy of the minister and of the traditions of the great party to which he once belonged.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member cannot laugh an argument down in that way. There is the fact, if my hon. friend is going to argue upon the point of custody. That is the fact; let my hon. friend argue on that point. To attempt to laugh down the argument will not affect it in any way.

Any document from the Dominion GoveromenU-when I say Dominion Government, I speak of officers appointed by the Dominion Government-must be printed in both languages, the Canada Gazette just as well as any other document.
Why, as a minister ot the Crown, did the hon. member not insist on this being done before?

There is no statute ot limitations against natural rights. If this clause passed unnoticed before my eyes during the last twenty-five years that I have been a member of this House, I plead guilty to that; but is that a reason or an argument why I should not plead that the clause should be amended in order to make it constitutional? The question was never raised before, it is true; but the question being raised to-night, and this being a right, why should I be prevented from advocating the restitution of that right, especially when it is demonstrated that in many constituencies there is a grievance and in many others there is the possibility of a grievance? Would my hon. friend refuse to that minority which is under a grievance the remedy which is at hand by amending this section? Surely my hon. friend has a more tender heart than that. What can he gain by refusing to give back to the minority what has not been claimed during the past twenty-five years? My hon. friend is interested in having a clean election; we are all interested in having the people of this country understand the meaning of the election, the whys and the wherefores of the election. We are only asking Parliament to enlighten the minority which does not understand one language. Oh, but, we are told, foreigners, immigrants who have come to Canada, might just, as well claim the same privilege. That is a very poor argument,-if it be intended as argument. The Galicians, the Germans-who by the way are better treated in Ontario than are the French Canadians-the Austrians, the Russians, were all immigrants who came to this country, knowing full well that their language had here, no special status. They knew the law of the land, and in the immigration leaflets, issued by the Department of Immigration, those immigrants were told that English and French were.the only two official languages of the land. Therefore, when they reached Canada and accepted the bounty of the Government in the form of thousands of acres of land in the western prairies, they knew full well

that their language had no special status. The case is surely different with your fellow-members of French descent.
I said a moment ago that I regret the spirit which rwas evinced this evening on the part of some hon. gentlemen as they approached this question. I know this is a vexed and delicate problem. No one cares to discuss those awkward questions. But, Sir, as I said a moment ago, the minority is always jealous of its rights and of its privileges, and it has reason to be nervous when we hear language such as we have heard this evening. Do you believe, Mr. Chairman, that this country can strive for peace and harmony, and therefore for progress and success from a national point of view, if at every moment the constitutional rights of the minority are challenged as they are being challenged by some members of this House. If that system prevails, you will not succeed in restoring harmony in this country, and God knows it needs harmony and concord. I have been in England, and not very long ago I was asked to speak of Canada from the French-C'anadian point of view by the President of the Empire Parliamentary Association. I said, "I have no mandate. I occupy no official position in my country which justifies your invitation, but if you insist I will accept. I will not distribute flowers and laurels. I will speak the truth." I was answered, "Sir, we expect you to speak the truth, and we are anxious to know the truth about Canada."
And did you?

Yes, Sir, I spoke the truth; and let me tell my hon. friend I would repeat here what I said in London in the hearing of the Speaker. Speaking in St. Stephen's Hall in London I gave an outline of the treatment which for the last twenty-five years has been meted out to the French-Canadian minority in the province of Ontario and in the province of Manitoba. And, Sir, next morning, to my surprise, I found that the great organ of public opinion in Great Britain, the London Times, approved with one reservation only, every word that I had said, and expressed regret, if not shame, that fellow-members of the British Empire were treated as they were in the province represented by my hon. friend from West Toronto. The press of Great Britain re-echoed the comments of the London Times, and statesmen of all parties, Whigs and Tories, Unionists and Coalitionists, all approved of my language. I can give a list of the guests who were present at that dinner. Mr. Chairman,

when, during that address, I stated, for instance, that just prior to the war the French-Canadian minority in the province of Ontario had been deprived of a privilege enjoyed since time immemorial-a privilege that was maintained in favour of the German minority-I was interrupted by this exclamation, "Is that possible in the province of Ontario?" I said "It is a fact."
They did not know conditions as well as we know them.
You know too much.

Ignorance, thou art
bliss! I shall at any time of the year and at any hour of the day take the judgment of plain John Bull of England in preference to the judgment of my hon. friend.
My hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General a moment ago questioned my statement as to the status of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Here is what I find in Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, page 188:
The Office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, consisting of three permanent officers and such temporary clerks as may be required from time to time. The clerk of the Crown in chancery is always present at the table of the House of Commons, at the commencement of a new parliament, and hands to the clerk the roll, or return book, which contains the list of members elected to serve in the parliament. In conformity with law he issues writs for elections, makes certificates to the house, in due form, of the return of members, and performs other functions relating to elections. He attends the house with election returns, and amends the same, when so ordered. The various proclamations, summoning, proroguing, and dissolving parliament, are issued by command out of chancery. He is also required to attend in the Senate Chamber at the close of a session, or whenever his Excellency the governor general gives the royal assent to bills, the titles of which it is the duty of this officer to read. Prom the foregoing summary of this officer's duties it will be seen that, while he is appointed by the Crown to perform certain duties by its command in connection with elections, and also to attend in the upper house on the occasion of the exercise of certain royal prerogatives, he is also an officer of the House of Commons. He must obey its orders to lay on the Table election returns In his possession and even alter them at its direction. The office was formerly specially attached to the privy council, but is now directly under the jurisdiction of the House of Commons.
That disposes of the argument of my hon. friend of a moment ago.
One word more and; I am done. I am too old in public life to raise any racial, sentimental, or religious issue, but I feel too much the dignity of my race to tolerate any slurs against it, especially when I know its history. I know too much of politics to be wedded in any slavish fashion to any party.

I am more of a Canadian than I am a Liberal, although I believe, Mr. Chairman, that being a good Liberal means being a good Canadian. I appeal to my fellow-members as f el 1 o w-C a nadi a n s to stop listening to such arguments as we have heard this evening from my hon. friend from West Toronto, my hon. friend from Fron-tenac, and my hon. friend from North Perth. Will the Government of Canada, if they want to be strong, accept at any little breeze the dictation of a few firebrands? Surely the Government of Canada has more dignity and more moral courage than that! Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from West Toronto expresses the hope that Quebec and the French Canadians and their institutions, educational and otherwise, may improve in the years to come-no doubt by contact with him and the institutions he represents. I believe, Sir, that a great deal can be done by daily contact between the two great races of this Dominion. I believe-and this has always been the ideal of my life; it has been my guiding star-that we have to learn one from the other. We must respect eaich other's virtues, we must respect, as stated this afternoon so wisely by my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), even our respective failings and prejudices. But, above all,, we must be Canadians. No one should hope that the minority in this country shall learn it all from the other. Surely that is not a healthy sentiment, and if perchance the hon. member for West Toronto believes that, with his narrow views and bigoted policies, as expressed in his paper, he can dispose of the so-called French-Cana-dian peril, he is completely at sea. Forgetting the intellectual point of view, forgetting the history of the French-iCanadians, forgetting their natural aptitudes to be something and somebody in this Canada of ours, let him remember these essential facts. At the time of the conquest in 1763 there were 65,000 French Canadians in Canada; at the time of the Union in 1640 there were about 500,000; in 1867 at the time of Confederation a little over 1,000,000; Sir, at the next census there will be at least 2,500,000 sturdy Canadians of French descent from one end of the country to the other, and there are over 1,000,000 of the same stock in the United States of America. If it be true that a healthy, law-abiding and God-fearing peoiple can double its numbers every thirty years, I predict to the hon. member for West Toronto and to his compeers in Toronto that in thirty years from
1921 his sons, or his grandsons, will awaken to find that there are 5,000,000 French-Can-adian people. In sixty years his grandsons will find, by the same process off the doubling of population every thirty years, thait there are in Canada 10,000,000 French-iCanadians, faithful to their Church, to their institutions, aye faithful to their language, assuredly because they thrive on persecution. Therefore it is useless, it is in vain, for my hon. friend by his campaign of vilification, to dream of wiping out that old and respectable population of 2,500,000 which, without any capital from abroad, without any aid from the ancient Mother country, relying only on its own courage, its own stability, its own love of the land of its ancestors, has maintained itself and progressed in such a remarkable way.
Sir, I appeal to the common sense, to the spirit of fair play which is in every British breast. I will say, in the words which were heard as a last command from the old captain of the "Titanic," addressing himself to his crew and the passengers as his ship was foundering, "Be British; be British!"
I look upon this as quite a pleasant evening-
Or morning.

-Morning. I have got more information than I ever got before. We have heard about this proolamation. I have voted a good many times, I have been all over this province, and I have yet to find the man who lost his vote because the proclamation was not in French. If there was a constituency in which there were French people who could not speak English, you would be very anxious to go there to inform them that there was a proclamation out and that there was going to be an election. You only seek to have this amendment adopted because you are in opposition now and it will be twenty years before you ever get in, and if I got 'my wish it would be a little longer still. You are in opposition because you are against everything no matter whether it is good or bad. You have been that ever since I have been a member of this House. I think we can hardly give praise enough to the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) for the way that he started our hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) to speak. That hon. gentleman commenced. with a great deal of wrath directed at the hon. member for West Toronto. He could hardly say anything bad enough about the hon. member. Hon. members find it necessary to

pursue that line of argument because they have not very much else to say on that side [DOT]of the House. I think the hon. member for West Toronto deserves a great deal of credit for telling us exactly where you (Mr. Lemieux) stand and what you are. You said that you were in Britain. I suppose you were in the House of Commons. You said that you were requested to speak, that you did speak and that the public applauded you. You made a great mistake when you did not stay there, because I do not think you will ever be applauded to any great extent in this country. Another thing that I took in a very good-natured way was the speech of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien). He went out of his way a good deal, and I never thought that one man could get down as low as he did. Tliere is only one in this House who could have done what he did in reading documents in regard to the Orange Lodge. There is one thing I would tell you, and that is that the great principle of the Orange Lodge is civil and religious liberty for all men. I want you to take note of that. I would hardly think it worth while to reply to the hon. member (Mr. Yien) because what he said came from so low a source that it is beneath me to pay any attention to it. The hon. gentleman talked in such a way that he could not get any reply to it. I want to tell my hon. friend when he talks about the smallness of the people on this side of the House and the bigotry of a certain class that I am an Orangeman,-
Hear, hear.
We know it.
-and that the principles of Orangemen are far above those held by my hon. friend. His principles are far to small to even measurably approach those of the members, of the Orange body.

How many of them are
there?

I expected to have heard
better things from some hon. gentlemen opposite. There is a little instrument over there that they call a " cannon." I have listened to it with a great deal of pleasure very often but there is no harm in it. It only gives utterance to bombast, and we do not pay any attention to it. What the "cannon" says would not hurt one anyway because it does not amount to very much. But there is one thing I do object to. I had a great deal of respect for my hon. friend over there, but I shall never have

the same respect for him again because he has done his best to create hard feeling in this Canada of ours. As a resident of this country, who knows the French fairly well, I have a very good opinion of them. But for that hon. gentleman to stand up in this House and try to create divisions between the two races is something I never expected him to do. Something has been said about the late Sir John Macdonald. I knew Sir John Macdonald very well, and I used to hear him on the hustings talking about the French. I heard him say that they had a lot of good habits " but," he says, " you cannot trust them."
I would not rise at this la'te hour to say even a word or two had it not been for some remarks made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve *(Mr. Lemieux).
Parlez Francais.

Non, monsieur. The remarks of that hon. gentleman led me to the thought that he has put the proposition on a totally different ground from that on which it was put by all the other members on that side who have spoken. We have been listening to what has been practically a bombardment by many hon. gentlemen opposite based on what they conceive to be the right which exists under the constitution. The hon. gentleman has waived that entirely to one side by claiming that the principle upon which he advocated that the proclamations should be published in French was following what he conceived to be a natural right that was implied, under all the legislation of the past from the Treaty of Paris down. Now in that way the hon. gentleman has really fallen in line with the argument-eited by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards)-laid down by Mr. Belcourt, a member I think of the Senate, and a prominent lawyer who has delivered himself at length upon that subject and in no unmistakable way. I only deal with that argument in the hope that it may do some good in the case of the younger members of the House who take issue with constitutional lawyers, men of long experience, and who set up a different construction of the law from what these men of experience adopt. Hon. gentlemen opposite outside of the argument as to the constitutional right have tried to put an interpretation upon section 133 which I do not think the section is capable of bearing. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) particularly, and I think the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon)

and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) and others, have tried to interpret section 133 in their own way so far as regards the words:
-and both languages shall be used in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve followed that argument to some extent; but none of these gentlemen have tried for a moment to put what would be the reasonable meaning upon these words. Now that seems to be the crux of the point and the only argument that is left to hon. gentlemen opposite, because it is conceded here that there is no legal right outside of the limits of section 133, and I think the House is pretty well agreed upon the territorial limits within which that territorial right can be exercised. There only remains then the question of the meaning of these words " Records and Journals of the House." I hold in my hand one of the Journals of this House, the official volume 55 for the year 1919-taken at random-which bears the caption "Journals of- the House of Commons of Canada." That is what is intended to be meant by the words of the section
Journals of the House of Commons of Canada This Journal has been printed since Confederation, and every copy can be found in the custody of the proper official of the House printed in both French and English. That is the Journal of the House of Commons.
Now the other question to be ascertained is what constitutes a " Record." We know what the Journal contains. It contains the minutiae of the daily proceedings of the House, everything that takes place from prayers at the opening right through the sitting, and everything that is tabled, is set forth in the Journals of the House.

My hon. friend knows
that there are certain things in the form of returns that are tabled and that are not included in the Journals of the House. Does he claim that these do not form part of the records of the House?

There is nothing that
is tabled that is not noted in the Journals of the House as having been laid upon the Table.

Even when it is not
printed?
There is a complete daily record in the Journals of the House of what takes place in the House.
But they are not printed.
They are printed.
Not all-
Absolutely.
Except by order of the House.

Everything is printed
especially when ordered by the House to be printed. When printed they form part of the records of the House, to a certain extent, and are shown in the Journals. The records consist of the sessional papers laid on the Table and these are most important. If ordered to be printed they are to be printed in French and English. The Hansard is also part of the records of the House being a record of everything that takes place viva voce in the Chamber. The stenographic notes are taken and then transcribed in French and English and are published through the medium of Hansard. The Bills are also part of the records of the House. The Bills that are introduced and passed, together with all their retspective changes-from the time of introduction to the final reading; to the stage when they receive their final assent in the Senate-are all noted and form part of the records of the House; and any hon. gentleman, if he desires, can go back to the earliest times-so far as this House is concerned-and in half an hour he can get any original document that is filed as of record in this Parliament from the custodian of those papers. These are the records.
Now the peculiarity is that the original of every Bill that gets the assent is engrossed on parchment in duplicate, one part in French and the other in English, and signed by the Governor in Council or the official acting for him in absentia; these are records also. And if we take the language of the section we shall find that the records and journals of the House are limited to what takes place in this House in the regular parliamentary way under parliamentary practice as detailed in the journals and files of record.
Let us look at the proclamation. The form, as far as the printed bill is concerned, becomes a record because it is in the Bill in draft form with blanks; but the proclamation that is issued by the electoral officer-under the old Act by the returning officer-never was in this Chamber, and under the election law as set forth in this Act never will be in this Chamber unless under souft remarkable and unusual circumstances, in which event it would be

tabled and in the custody of the House. Then it would become a record of the House and would be printed in French and English because it was a record long after the election based on the proclamation had been held.
Let us see how far a little further argument along that line will bring us. Hon. gentlemen opposite argue that because it is ordered by the House therefore it is a record of the House. As I have already shown, it never was in the House, it never had an entity, it never was a paper tabled, it never had any meaning as being in the House in the form published. The returning officer has to keep the results of his election after sending in his return, and the only thing that is of record in the House is the return sent in by that officer of the election or of the return of a member. That is read by the Speaker from the Chair, it is taken down by Hansard, and the return is taken note of for the dally journal of the House. But the returning officer has to keep all the papers-I am speaking in a general way and from mem-ory-for one year, and in the case of a contested election as I read the Act for another year if that year be about expired, or for a year from the time the protest was lodged. I asked the hon. member for Three *Rivers (Mr. Bureau) to-night what would become of those papers then? He replied: Why, he could destroy them if he liked. Is the hon. gentleman serious in suggesting that an official authorized to perform certain functions can of his own will destroy records of this House? No! He destroys them because they never were records of this House and never were intended to be; they are in his custody to do what he likes with after the statutory period has expired.
What about during the statutory period?

During the statutory
period the returning officer is to keep possession of these papers-that is what the law says. That is long after the election is held, long after the publication of the proclamation, and the operations of the Act have been fulfilled by the publication of the proclamation followed by the election of the returned member. So it is absolutely futile to argue that a mere proclamation is a part of the journals or records of this House.
Let me go a step further. There is a protest, and incidental to the protest, we will assume for the moment, the returning officer was compelled under a subpoena duces

tecem to produce the proclamation to the rota of judges trying the election petition. Being so produced it becomes a part of the records of the court. Since when has it been recognized that the records of Parliament may be handled under a subpoena duces tecem through the medium of a man who is not appointed as an official of this House to take under his control documents of that kind? The returning officer producing that paper, the moment that the trial is over, may by virtue of his right say to the court: The exhibit I filed belongs to me.
I have a statutory duty to keep it for a year. He may make application for the return of the exhibit, which the court may or may not grant according to the circumstances. But assuming he is allowed to take it off the files of the court, he takes that paper back, and probably there may be some reason why in the strict observance of his duties he must keep it a s'till longer time until the statutory period is ended.

May I be permitted a remark? I do not know what the practice of the Ontario Courts is, but before our courts in Quebec never in my experience has the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery parted With the possession of the documents in connection with an election. He produces them before the court, but he keeps them in his possession.

It just makes my argument that much stronger, that neither the court nor any other authority has any right to the papers since there is a statutory obligation upon that man to keep them and, as my hon. friend from Three Rivers says, to destroy them after the statutory period is ended. To argue that they are records of the House is absolutely beside the question.

I approach this matter
without any prejudice whatever, inasmuch as I do not belong to the Orange Order, nor yet have I been taken into the fold of the Roman Catholic Church. Consequently anything I may say will be entirely free from bias, and as such I think ought to be listened to by the committee with a willing ear.
If I may be permitted to give some advice to the Government, I would suggest that in this matter, .assuming that there is no right whatever with regard to the use of the French language, the Government ought for political and diplomatic reasons to go a little distance with the province of Quebec. The Government is woefully weak in Quebec representation-that is, numerically. Prac-

tically the entire contingent from Quebec has received seats in the Cabinet-or something just as good. I refer to the position which is now being occupied by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames). Nohting was too good for Quebec. Three seats are held by supporters of the Government from Quebec, and these gentlemen were considered so worthy that two of them are now numbered among the advisers of the King and the other gentleman is in Geneva.
What about the Postmaster General?

I did not say anything
about the Postmaster General because he is not a member of this House, and I cannot refer to the other House. What I wish to say is that if the Government desires to strengthen its position in Quebec it is certainly not taking the proper course. This by way of a bit of advice to the Government.
The name of Sir John Macdonald was used here to night by the member for Carleton (Mr. Boyce) and I am sorry that he is not in his seat at the present moment. He made the statement that Sir John Macdonald confided to him that " he could not trust the French of Quebec."
Sir John may or may not have made that statement; he is not here to deny it. Perhaps the statement was made such a long time ago that the memory of my hon. friend from Carleton is a little hazy about it. But Sir John Macdonald never had any reason to make a statement of that kind, because he trusted Quebec, and that trust was returned a hundredfold. He held office for many years because he was able to control the province of Quebec, and, at the same time, the Orange Order of Ontario. Now, that was quite a feat. Inasmuch as my hon. friends opposite find that they have practically no representation from Quebec, may I suggest, in spite of the statement made by the member for Carleton, that it would be wise for the Government to see to it that the Quebec representation is strengthened on their side of the House? At present the Government is what I would call a jug-handled government. One-third of the population of this country is not represented on the other side of the House. How is it possible for a government to govern under such conditions,? As a matter of politics I suggest to to the minister that even at the last moment he might very well consider the remarks which were made on this side and go a certain length in order to see to it that 147
these-I will not call them rights; call them privileges if you like-are granted to our friends of the province of Quebec.'
Now, kfter all, what is it that is asked? We say that if it is impossible for the people living in a certain community to understand the language of the proclamation, that proclamation ought to be published in the language which they understand. Is that an unreasonable request? I say it is not. Why, if you buy a bottle of patent medicine you will find that the directions for use are published in about fifteen different languages, whereas in the matter of a proclamation under the Franchise Act, a matter which vitally affects the people, this right to read in a language which they understand is denied to the people.
Efforts have been made during the last year or two to conciliate the province of Quebec in a number of ways. The newspapers of the Government of late, instead of roaring like lions, have been roaring as gently as sucking doves, about Quebec. Now, what is the object? The object is to conciliate Quebec and attempt to obtain some representation without which this Government can not live. We heard about the little excursion which was made down the St. Lawrence by the Prime Minister and one or two of his friends in search' of some new cabinet material. Many of us were on our guard; we were afraid that the hen roost was going to be robbed. Some people thought that the Prime Minister was aiming at no less a person than Sir Lomer Gouin, and other names were mentioned later when it was found that Sir Lomer was not to be attracted by the offers of the Prime Minister. Now, this goes to show that a determined effort is being made to secure representation foT the province of Quebec. Yet when an opportunity is given of in some way conciliating the province of Quebec the Acting Solicitor General refuses pointlblank to take advantage of it. He said that his views were rather in favour of the suggested amendment, but that there were others who were against it. Perhaps I imay be permitted to use the language which has been made current in this House by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) when speaking on another matter he said that it was a case of " passing the buck," whatever that means. The Canada Gazette is published in two languages, English and french. The 'Canada Gazette is not a document of the House or a journal of the House. It circulates from Prince Edward



Island to Vancouver Island. The Acting Solicitor General, I understand, has told us that there is nothing in the law which makes it necessary to publish these things in the two languages; that that has only been done as a matter of convenience,- purely by complaisance. If that is the case, he has a precedent for saying to-day that these proclamations are published as a matter of convenience and in that way giving satisfaction to everyone. Had I my way I would be in favour of publishing that proclamation in every language spoken within the confines of this Dominion. I would publish it in Scandinavian, in German, even in Yiddish; I would publish it in every language known, because after 'all the object of the proclamation is to give the citizens of this 'Country information as to what they are to do and where they are to vote. What is there wrong about that? If it i!s a matter of convenience; if it is essential that we should have reflected in this House the opinion of everyone in this community no matter what language he speaks, why is it that we restrict the publication of the proclamation to the English language and in certain particular places allow its publication also in French? There is no reason in the wide world, for instance, why the county of Glengarry, where nearly fifty per cent of the people are French Canadian, should not have these proclamations published in French. There is no reason why in the counties of Prescott, Russell and others, the proclamations should not be in French as well as in English. No valid reason has been urged by the Acting Solicitor General why this should not be done. Speaking for myself, as I say, without any prejudice whatever, I think that the Government is making a serious mistake, for diplomatic and political reasons if for no higher object, in denying the rights which are asked for by members on this side.

In reply to the member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), I think I can throw some light on the situation if I quote from the French version of the British North America Act, Section 133 says:
(Translation) :
Either the English or the French language may he used by any person in the Debates of the Houses of the Parliament of Canada and of the Houses of the (Legislature of Quebec, and both those languages shall be used in the respective Records. .	.	.
And this is the point, Mr. Chairman, that I wish to emphasize:
[ Mr. Jacobs. ]
.	.	. And both those languages shall be used
in the respective Records and Journals of those Houses.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what is it that constitutes records? These records- are documents which are intrusted to an officer of the House of Commons, under an Act of Parliament, in order that they become part of the records of this House, so that subsequently they can be used for some purpose. This Bill provides that an officer of this House, appointed under the law, shall keep those documents during a fixed period. If the man is not obliged to keep those papers indefinitely, it is because we allow him, under the 1 aw or implicitly, the privilege to destroy them as soon as the period during which he is bound to preserve them has come to an end. Consequently, the word " used " applies to the papers which are intrusted to an officer of the House of Commons in order that they may be used subsequently for some -purpose. Now, Mr. Chairman, according to the definition which I have given to-day, the English word " records " means all the documents which might subsequently be used as evidence when an election is contested before the courts of justice. You cannot give another interpretation to section 75 of this Bill.
To prevent the accumulation of records in the House and to make their destruction a matter of course, once their usefulness is gone, they are given into the custody of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery during a certain period. I submit that our election documents are not records of the House because of the duration of this custody but because of the fact- itself that they are given into the custody of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery; because of the fact that it is precisely this officer who has charge of them, and because of the fact that the law requires this very thing.
We have appointed an officer who, linden the law, must keep certain documents that have to do with an election. The proof of an election is the proclamation stating that the election is to take place. Without such a -proclamation there can be no proof that an election has been held. The first thing that must be established to the satisfaction of the court, in an election dispute, is the fact that an election has been held, and since this evidence is necessary and must be submitted before the proceedings can continue, the proclamation belongs with the other documents that, according to the interpretation clause just quoted, are styled election documents. I claim that, according to the French version of the constitution, all election documents are

records of the House and must be printed in the two official languages, French and Fnglish. I fail to see how we can possibly escape from the horns of that dilemma and say that, for the purposes of this Act, the records shall not he records, so as to allow of these gentlemen accomplishing whatever objects they may have in view.
Mr, d'ANJOU (Rimouski). (Translation): Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to detain the committee very long at this late hour, but I cannot let the debate come to a close without saying a few words. After listening with attention to the speeches made in the House, particularly to those of my hon. friends on this side, I have come to the conclusion that the election proclamations which we are discussing are just as much a part of the records of the House as are the Votes and Proceedings, the Debates, etc., and consequently that they should be printed in both the official languages of this country.
The hon. member for 'St. James (Mr. Rin-fret) in the magnificent speech he delivered to the committee introduced a new argument into the discussion, an argument which, it seems to me, deserves consideration. The bon. member from 'St. James, sjeaking of the Naturalization Act of 1919, demonstrated to the House that every alien desirous of becoming naturalized must, besides being otherwise qualified, possess a satisfactory knowledge of either the French or the English tongue.
Now, since to vote at a federal election one must be naturalized and since one of the requisites of naturalization is a knowledge of either the French or English, I cannot understand why the Government of Canada should not publish the election proclamations in both the official languages of this country. The Naturalization Act states that in order to be admitted to citizenship one must have a knowledge of either the English or French language; there is no mention of German, nor of any other foreign tongue. The law thus acknowledges the rights of the French tongue in this country.
I shall give my utmost support to the amendment of the hon. member from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon). If I were to offer any word of criticism it would be that his motion is altogether too tame. In so far as I, personally, am concerned, what I am asking the Parliament of Canada for is not a favour, neither is it a privilege; I am demanding the recognition of a right granted our language by the Constitution of this country. I cannot understand why the 147i
Government refuses to accept this motion, so eloquently seconded by all the hon. members on this side of the House who spoke here to-day.
Mr. Chairman, in order to strengthen my argument, I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the following resolution which has been on the Order Paper for some time under the name of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach):
That, in the opinion of this House, all newspapers, pamphlets, advertisements, political campaign literature, and publications of like nature, printed and published in Canada, or distributed or circulated in Canada, in a language other than the English or French language, should not be permitted to be circulated or distributed unless such publications hear, in parallel columns, a translation of the same in the English or French language.
That only goes to show Mr. Chairman, that there is no question in Canada of the German, or any other tongue and that the equality of rights between the French and English languages in this country is not only acknowledged in an official way, but that it is admitted even by those who dis-, pute our right to speak the French tongue. The argument, it seems to me, is not without worth since it shows that those who pretend to ignore it are forced to recognize the fact that, in Canada, French and English are equal before the law.
If the English language were the only official language used in this country, why ,should the hon. member for Edmonton not have mentioned the fact that those printed documents and advertisements should be translated into English only, and why should he not have asked that they be translated into German or into any other language?
Mr. Chairman, this shows that the French language as well as the English language, is here to stay, no matter what may be done against it. I do not intend to retain the attention of the House for any further length of time. I considered it my duty, before the debate was at an end, to say a few words in support of this amendment. Unfortunately, the question had been decided beforehand; it is obvious that the Government has yielded to the Orange pack, and eager as it is to please those gentlemen under any circumstances, it has made up its mind not to grant this request submitted by hon. members in the name of the French speaking population of this country towards securing the recognition of a certain right. It seems to me that to speak French when vindicating this right is an

excellent means of showing that we are entitled to use that language in Canada, in this House and out of it as well, and that the best means of preserving a right is to make use of it. Wherefore I have, spoken in French, to-night, as I usually do, and it was only natural that I should have done so, because I had risen to vindicate the rights of Her Majesty the French tongue.

I did not expect that
the amendment which I moved would have raised such a debate in this House of Commons of Canada. The debate which has taken place this evening has certainly won my admiration, and although once in a while the discussion may have waxed a little strong between a couple of members on either side of the House, I must say that the lesson taught the country by the speeches which have been delivered on both sides will convince the people of Canada, as it has strengthened me in my conviction, of the truth of the principle that a bilingual Parliament can exist only in a bilingual country. If the members of the IHbuse had not felt that we were living in a bilingual country, this House would have adjourned before twelve o'clock. I am confirmed in my conviction, in spite of what has been said by some hon. gentlemen opposite, that seventy-five per cent of the English population of the Dominion are in favour of the amendment which I have moved, and will consider that this is merely an acknowledgement of a right acquired, a privilege which everybody is willing to give to a minority which is willing to accept with such pleasure and gratitude every possible privilege accorded to it. I have been castigated by some hon. members opposite because some years have elapsed and because a similar amendment was not brought in in the election of 1911, or of 1908, or of 1904. The old law, which has been on the statute book for many years, was framed in accordance with the mentality of the people at that time, and no opportune time arose for any member of Parliament, who wished to maintain the prevailing spirit of harmony, to move the amendment which I am moving to-day. Now when the Government is introducing a new franchise law, which will be on the statute book for future elections, which may come in three months or three years, and which law will remain on the statute book for years to come it is an opportune time for any hon. member who desires to have the law amended, to bring in his
IMr. d'Anjou.]	.
amendment. The war is over and we are now engaged on the work of reconstruction, and I think reconstruction in matters of harmony and concord should be the first consideration. As I said before, in the twenty years I have been in Parliament I have never advocated extreme measures. I have, however, always expressed my views, and if at times they may have been stronger than at others my actions have always been dictated by a sense of duty and conviction. There is to-day greater proportion of the French element in the Dominion of Canada than existed thirty or forty years ago, and these people have, according to my conviction, the same rights in the matter of language in matters of Federal concern as the English-speaking people. It has been stated that some English-speaking people in the province of Ontario might be offended to have to read a proclamation in French. I do not see why they should be any more offended at that, than at receiving a postal order, which is invariably printed in both languages;-the only offence they could take would be that it was too small in amount. I do not wish at this time to do anything to create disunion, and I am prepared to withdraw the amendment which I have placed on Hansard and which has been debated to-night. I have listened with great pleasure to one of my old leadrs of the Liberal party, whom it has been my pleasure to follow for years in this House, just as I followed him with pleasure in his past career in the Maritime Provinces, where he had been a figure long before he entered this Parliament in 1896. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, ex-Minister of Finance in the Laurier Government, while not finding fault with my amendment, recognizes, however, that there are tw7o views in this country as to the rights of the French language, and in order not to offend one school of thought he has suggested an amendment which might possibly be more acceptable to hon. gentlemen opposite. He has read his suggestion, and I am willing to withdraw my amendment and substitute for it the suggested amendment of my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's.

speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the committee that the hon. gentlelman have leave to withdraw his amendment?
Amendment withdrawn.

I beg to move to amend clause 37 by adding at the end of subclause (1) the following words:
Provided however that in any electoral district in which, to the knowledge of the returning offi-

cer, there is a considerable number of electors who are familiar with the French language but do not understand the English language, the proclamation shall be issued in both languages.
Amendment negatived; yeas -38, nays 63.
